author: Erica Malatesta
title: The May Elections and After: The Labour Leadership Contest
content:
Photo: Keir Burnham, oops, Andy Starmer

The May councillor and mayoral elections showed the shifting ground of British politics. The two main establishment parties, Labour and the Conservatives, were decimated, and many, well those who bothered to vote, did so against the attacks both had led against working conditions and living standards of the working class.  This disgust was expressed in Wales and in Scotland with votes for the nationalist parties, which adopt centrist to left social democratic language.  Labour lost almost 1500 council seats, in England, whilst the Tories, with a much reduced 1,300 seats, lost a further 600 seats.

However, the biggest benefactors were the far-right populists of Reform, who won roughly 30% of the council seats up for grabs, including 14 councils. These included traditional Labour strongholds like Barnsley, Gateshead, and Sandwell. They came second after the Plaid Cymru nationalists in Wales and in Scotland grabbed 16% of the vote.

Farage and Reform are exploiting the anger felt by many with successive Tory and Labour governments, and fanning the flames of racism in British society.  Many were disgusted with the way the Starmer government carried on with austerity measures like previous Tory governments. The vote for Reform appears to be higher in the most deprived areas.  On the other hand, some working class voters voted tactically to block Reform. This wasn’t by any means a guaranteed vote for Labour, as the Greens won 500 councillors, an increase of more than 400.

In fact, the Greens seem to be filling the vacuum of social-democracy relinquished by Labour, with increasingly left-sounding promises. The nationalists of Plaid Cymru and the SNP use similar rhetoric to gain working class votes. Zack Polanski referred to the Greens as the ‘workers party’, and put forward a charter for workers.

However, like Green Parties in other parts of the world, and indeed with already sitting Green councillors and councils in the UK, the hopes of the Green Party posing a genuine alternative will soon be dashed. In over 40 councils they have helped implement cuts just like the rest. Where they now have wrested control, will they refuse to implement austerity measures?

Well, Polanski has said that councils have no choice in implementing cuts because it’s due to the decisions of central government. No mention of local organising of workers and local people in alliance with intransigent councillors, or a cartel of councils pledging to refuse to implement cuts. This doesn’t even enter his head!

The Labour government is deeply unpopular as a result of its first two years, where it attacked pensioners and pursued policies that showed it was jettisoning any idea of welfarism and left rhetoric. It blatantly is pro-business and pro-market.

Starmer sought to block any contenders to leadership of Labour back in 2021 when he increased the percentage of MPs needed to set off a contest from 10% to 20%. This has blocked the former Health Secretary Wes Streeting, himself an alternative Starmer, with a record of viciously attacking the NHS, and indeed, if anything, more Blairite than Starmer.

Sections of the Labour Party are panicking that under Starmer they will lose the next election. They are looking to Andy Burnham, Mayor of Greater Manchester, as someone to replace Starmer.

Andy Burnham is no fiery left winger. He supported the Iraq war when he was a MP, voting for the invasion of Iraq. He served as a minister under Blair, and over the next ten years he voted to block any independent inquiry into the war. He then opportunistically started to say that he regretted the war when he became Mayor of Manchester.​ Whilst in Parliament, he abstained on opposing welfare cuts proposed by the Tory government. He made it abundantly clear when Corbyn was elected Labour leader, that he was dissociating himself from the whole phenomenon of Corbynism. He supported Starmer in the 2020 leadership contest.

In addition, he was an important member of Labour Friends of Israel whilst in parliament, and has spoken regularly at their events. He says that Israel would be the first country he would visit if he became Prime Minister. He is a confirmed supporter of the Zionist state.

Now, however, in order to win the leadership election, (that is if he is actually elected MP in Makerfield) he has to pose as to the left of Starmer. So, he is calling for more funding for council housing and more re-nationalisation (indeed Starmer himself is changing direction over this, now calling for nationalisation of the steel industry).

Sections of the ruling class are concerned that Starmer cannot retain control over his MPs and continue its assaults on the working class. Therefore, Burnham is seen as a handy alternative, due to his supposed popularity, and better able to implement harsh measures. Burnham has said that he supports fiscal rules and so may well curry favour with sections of the boss class. He hopes to garner the racist vote by his support for anti-migrant action pushed by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood. He has said that the government should spend more on defence, rather than health, education and infrastructure.

The past few decades of austerity and rising cost of living have dealt severe blows to the old establishment parties of Labour and Conservatives. Unfortunately, the vacuum that is opening does not benefit truly radical ideas, but offers new opportunities for the populist far right. Bigotry and racism are now fully out in the open. As for the left, whether they be the old Stalinist formations or the Trotskyist groups, they have been unable to develop any significant threat, tied as they are by an umbilical cord to Labourism. The majority of British anarchism, now much reduced, is also similarly unable to offer a challenge.

A social alternative is in dire need of being created. This has to mean painstaking work around the cost-of-living crisis, the rising cost of energy and food, housing, and transport. This crisis has been aggravated by the Trump regime’s war against Iran, and so a clear antimilitarist message has to be linked to any such fight against this crisis. Whether this alternative can be built remains to be seen. If not, the far right will profit.

The Anarchist Communist Group (ACG) is a revolutionary class struggle organisation, set up in February 2018.

author: ROAPE
title: Honouring a fallen warrior
content:
In this obituary, Jabu Nala-Hartley remembers leading South African labour militant, trade unionist and socialist David Hemson. To learn more about his life and legacy, you can watch David in conversation here with ROAPE’s Peter Dwyer, discussing working class politics and the struggle against apartheid in South Africa.

When someone recently asked me if I was alright, I almost gave the familiar answer: “Yes, I’m fine.” But the truth is, I was not. Because how can any of us be fine when our movement has lost David Hemson – a giant of the workers’ struggle, a comrade whose spirit shaped generations?

This is a moment when words cannot fail us. When a warrior bows, we must rise to honour the truth he lived for.

I am Jabu Nala-Hartley, daughter of Junerose Nala, General Secretary of the Metal and Allied Workers’ Union in South Africa from 1976 to 1983. I am a former Oxford City councillor, former Chair of Oxford Labour, and once a challenger for the Oxford East parliamentary seat. My political consciousness was shaped by the very movement that David helped build.

David was my mother’s comrade in the early South African trade union movement. Through her, and through her friend Ntokozo Mbhele  – both fearless trade unionists of the 1970s and 1980s  – I was adopted into a circle of solidarity that shaped my life.

Their comradeship was not theoretical. It was forged in the fires of real struggle: the strikes of the 1970s; the drafting of legislation to protect workers; the battles against unsafe factory conditions; and the confrontations with bosses shielded by apartheid’s machinery of oppression.

These were people prepared for imprisonment, even death, to see workers liberated.

In those years, white students stood shoulder to shoulder with black workers, defying segregation to build one of the most formidable labour movements in our history. The apartheid state tried to silence black voices through detentions and brutality, but David and his comrades led strikes so powerful they brought the economic machine to its knees.

From that struggle emerged a revolutionary guard of workers, united across racial lines, bound by purpose, and determined to dismantle the exploitative cheap-labour system.

David Hemson was not simply a trade union leader; he was a force of nature. His resilience was unmatched, his energy seemingly endless. I remember watching him in meetings, his eyes alive with conviction, his voice carrying the weight of workers who had no voice of their own. His spirit was uncrushable, and you could feel it the moment he entered a room.

It is no surprise that he walked alongside giants: Steve Bantu Biko, Rick Turner, Helen Bolton, June Rose Nala, BK Dladla, David Davy, Halton Cheadle, Bella, Mampisi, Sbongile, Mkhulu Thizi, Obed, Zuma, Alphius Mthethwa, Omar Bashir Mobbs, and many others.

These were people who lived the struggle, who were prepared to die for workers’ dignity. David belonged among them – not only because of his courage, but because of his humanity.

One moment will stay with me forever. In a meeting, David stood up and declared himself a Zulu warrior. The room fell silent. The English, the Irish, the Scottish, the Welsh, the Americans all looked puzzled. But I understood.

He was reaching back to his childhood in the Valley of a Thousand Hills outside Durban, to the warriors whose spirit shaped his own. In that moment, he reminded us that struggle is not only political – it is cultural, personal, lived. That was David: fearless, rooted, unafraid to claim his identity in the fight for workers everywhere.

David’s revolutionary consciousness was global. He connected workers across continents, bringing a sense of comradeship that knew no borders. One of his greatest joys was the 50-year commemoration of the 1973 strikes – a reminder of the victories that shaped our history and the sacrifices that made them possible.

Today, I grieve. I grieve for the man, the comrade, the friend. But I also carry his example with me. David Hemson showed us what it means to live for something bigger than yourself. His spirit lives on: in every worker who refuses to bend; in every voice raised against injustice; in every act of courage that keeps the struggle alive.

David taught us that struggle is not a burden – it is a duty, and it is a privilege.

Long live the defiant spirit of David Hemson. Long live. Amandla!

David was a great guy and a formidable leader I and many others were privileged to have work alongside him.

I am deeply moved by your words.
I met David Hamson for only a short time, but it was a decisive moment. I had lost my job after fighting for fellow workers, and I was ready to give up. I no longer believed change was possible.
David’s encouragement gave me the strength to stand up again. That strength carried me through a three-year battle with the Labour Commissioner. Today, that fight is finished, and I await the ruling.

David left something in me that I will never forget. I know every activist he taught will carry his legacy forward. We cannot give up.

May David Hamson’s spirit continue to guide us. From here in Namibia, I assure you: he will not be forgotten. Let us honor him on International Activists Day, alongside all those he fought with.

Thankyou for a wonderful tribute to a great comrade, an inspiration

Well said Jabu! I think of you both as Zulu warriors! I first met him in England, and got to know him and other SA comrades in exile and later I was visiting David, his parents and his brothers in the valley of a thousand hills,  when Nelson Mandela left Robben Island, the first step, we all hoped,  towards freedom & democracy. Vivien Walsh.

What a wonderful short blog/celebration of the incredible David Hemson – sadly I met him only once, but that a sense of working class power and capacity he always imparted. David was unyielding, and had experienced – what too few of us have – working class power and potential in action.

author: Unknown
title: Апелляционный суд утвердил приговор анархисту Руслану Сидики: 29 лет заключения
content:
1 июля Апелляционный военный суд в подмосковной Власихе оставил без изменений приговор анархисту Руслану Сидики. По сообщению проекта «Огни свободы», теперь приговор вступил в законную силу.

Руслан приговорили к 29 годам заключения: первые 9 лет — в тюрьме, затем 20 лет — в колонии строгого режима. Также ему назначены штраф в 2 миллиона рублей и 2 года ограничения свободы после освобождения.

Руслана осудили за атаку беспилотниками на военный аэродром Дягилево под Рязанью, подрыв грузового поезда на перегоне Рыбное — Блокпост 204 и подготовку еще одной предполагаемой акции на железной дороге. Суд квалифицировал первые 2 эпизода как теракты, совершенные в составе «организованной группы» с представителями украинских спецслужб.

При этом самый большой отдельный срок — 18 лет — Руслан получил не за подрыв поезда и не за атаку на аэродром, а по статье о «прохождении обучения в целях осуществления террористической деятельности». Следствие утверждало, что весной 2023 года Руслан проходил такое обучение в Турции и Латвии.

Защита указывала, что Руслан задолго до этих поездок самостоятельно интересовался химией, электроникой и беспилотниками, собирал квадрокоптеры и имел навыки изготовления взрывчатых устройств. Поэтому встречи за границей, по позиции защиты, были проверкой уже имевшихся знаний и лояльности, а не обучением чему-то новому.

Защита также требовала переквалифицировать эпизоды с аэродромом и железной дорогой с «терактов» на диверсии. Руслан не отрицал, что совершил эти акции, но подчеркивал: их целью были военные объекты и военная логистика, а не запугивание гражданского населения.

Атака на Дягилево была направлена на самолеты, участвовавшие в войне против Украины. По эпизоду с железной дорогой Руслан говорил, что хотел нарушить перевозки военных грузов и техники. Машинисты поезда получили ссадины, не повлекшие вреда здоровью, однако суд счёл, что взрыв создал опасность их гибели и других тяжких последствий.

Руслан также отрицал подготовку третьего взрыва. Суд признал его виновным в приготовлении к этой акции на основании переписки, съемки участка железной дороги и найденных при обыске веществ и компонентов. Защита указывала, что эти компоненты были приобретены до предыдущего подрыва, а доказательств начала сборки нового устройства нет.

В апелляции Руслан вновь заявил о пытках после задержания, передаёт «Медиазона» из зала суда: рассказал, что его пытали током, вынуждая оговорить себя, и заставляли подписывать пустые листы. Он также повторил, что не считает свои действия терактами и называл их диверсиями против военных объектов.

На заседании присутствовал представитель итальянского консульства: Руслан имеет гражданства России и Италии.

После того, как документы из суда поступят в СИЗО, Руслана отправят этапом в одну из 7 российских тюрем. До этого он, как предполагают «Огни свободы», еще около месяца будет находиться в СИЗО.

391999, Рязанская обл., г. Ряжск, ул. Красная, д. 1а, СИЗО-2, Сидики Руслан Касемович 1988 г. р. Возможна отправка писем через севисы «Ф-письмо», PrisonMail.Online (для иностранных карт) и «Зонателеком» (доступна оплата иностранной картой).

author: Isabel Ortega
title: Continúan agresiones contra la comunidad indígena autónoma de San Lorenzo de Azqueltán
content:
Fotos por Victor Ibarra / IMDEC

En días pasados, tras una reunión entre autoridades estatales, la comunidad de Azqueltán, en Jalisco, de nuevo sufrió el intento de despojo de uno de los predios que integran su territorio. Este hecho se suma a una serie de agravios sucedidos desde semanas atrás que ponen en riesgo a esta comunidad indígena.

San Lorenzo de Azqueltán, en Jalisco, es una comunidad Wixárika y Tepehuana que desde hace diez años lucha por el reconocimiento de su territorio ancestral y contra el despojo que pretenden realizar pequeños propietarios y ejidatarios de la zona. En los años que llevan defendiendo su territorio, han sufrido una serie de agresiones escaladas que han llegado a arrebatarle la vida a personas de la comunidad. En los últimos días, el despojo y el hostigamiento se han hecho presentes de nuevo en el territorio.

A través de un comunicado difundido por el Congreso Nacional Indígena, el pasado 26 de junio la comunidad denunció que recientemente se ha vivido un clima de máxima tensión, así como una serie de amenazas en su contra que han ido escalando.

En primer lugar, la comunidad denuncia que desde los primeros días de junio, un policía municipal de Villa Guerrero de nombre Efraín Reyes, presuntamente por orden de ejidatarios, colocó una puerta obstruyendo el paso del camino que conduce a un pozo de agua conocido como El Tacuache, el cual representa la única fuente de agua para consumo humano de la comunidad de Azqueltán. Los comuneros señalan que esta acción arbitraria vulnera sus derechos humanos y les despoja de un bien común que forma parte de sus tierras comunales.

De acuerdo a Quetzal Prado, abogada de la comunidad, el pozo El Tacuache se encuentra a escasos diez metros del río Bolaños, por lo que la acción de bloquear el acceso a él, además de ser un despojo para la comunidad, representa una violación a la Ley Nacional de Aguas.

Por otro lado, en días pasados se llevo a cabo una reunión donde participaron autoridades del estado de Jalisco, así como representantes de la comunidad de Azqueltán y ejidatarios opositores a la comunidad, con el objetivo de establecer acuerdos para evitar confrontaciones en el territorio en disputa. Sin embargo, en su comunicado la comunidad señala que al día siguiente de esta reunión, un grupo de personas, encabezadas por Fabián Reyes Márquez, acudieron a un predio comunal llamado La Peña Blanca, el cual históricamente ha pertenecido la comunidad de Azqueltán, para intentar tomar posesión de él.

En el predio se encontraban trabajando comuneros Wixaritari y Tepehuanos de la comunidad, a quienes el grupo invasor amenazó con llevarlos a la cárcel, bajo el argumento de que al tomar posesión del predio, estaban siguiendo indicaciones de la Dirección de Asuntos Agrarios del Gobierno del Estado de Jalisco. De esta manera, las personas agresoras amenazaron a los comuneros con que llamarían a la policía para que los “levantaran”. Días más tarde este mismo grupo de personas volvió a ingresar al predio, donde retiró los postes y el alambrado colocado por comuneros de Azqueltán, y se llevó dichos materiales.

En su comunicado, la comunidad de Azqueltán responsabilizó al gobierno de Jalisco por su falta de compromiso para detener y prevenir la violencia que continuamente amenaza a la comunidad; así como denunció a las instituciones gubernamentales por promover la confrontación y permitir la impunidad.

Es importante recordar que la violencia contra los comuneros de Azqueltán cobró la vida de su representante agrario, Marcos Aguilar Rojas, en noviembre del año pasado, asesinato cometido, de acuerdo al último comunicado de la comunidad, por el mismo grupo que hoy intenta apoderarse del predio La Peña Blanca. Así mismo, otros comuneros han sido violentados en el pasado, quedando con secuelas de por vida, como señalan los hallazgos de la Misión Civil de Observación convocada por la Red Nacional de Organismos Civiles de Derechos Humanos (Red TDT) realizada en mayo pasado.

Para Quetzal Prado, abogada de la comunidad, existe el riesgo latente de que las agresiones hacia la comunidad sigan escalando ante la inacción de las autoridades de Jalisco: “Lo que nos preocupa es que vaya a ir escalando nuevamente y que se sigan incrementando esas situaciones de provocación o de despojo, por lo que resulta necesario que las acciones del gobierno sean tendientes a castigar este actuar ilegal por parte de las personas del ejido”, señaló la abogada, en entrevista con Avispa Mídia.

Ante las nuevas agresiones, la comunidad exige el cese de todo intento de despojo, así como que el gobierno de Jalisco tome acciones inmediatas para frenar una posible escalada de violencia en su territorio. De igual manera, los comuneros demandan de que se retire inmediatamente la puerta que bloquea el acceso al pozo El Tacuache, así como respeto absoluto a su territorio comunal. Por último, en el comunicado, la comunidad exige justicia por asesinato del comunero Marcos Aguilar Rojas, y la reparación integral de los daños realizados en la última agresión.

El 26 de junio pasado, comuneros de Azqueltán recuperaron la posesión del predio invadido, donde continúan trabajando por acuerdo de su asamblea. En este contexto, la comunidad llama a las redes que les han acompañado, así como a la sociedad civil, a permanecer pendientes de los sucesos de los próximos días y a alzar la voz frente a los intentos de despojo de su territorio.

En este contexto, la comunidad llama a las redes que les han acompañado, así como a la sociedad civil, a permanecer pendientes de los sucesos de los próximos días y a alzar la voz frente a los intentos de despojo de su territorio.

author: Isabel Ortega
title: Continúan agresiones contra la comunidad indígena autónoma de San Lorenzo de Azqueltán
content:
Fotos por Victor Ibarra / IMDEC

En días pasados, tras una reunión entre autoridades estatales, la comunidad de Azqueltán, en Jalisco, de nuevo sufrió el intento de despojo de uno de los predios que integran su territorio. Este hecho se suma a una serie de agravios sucedidos desde semanas atrás que ponen en riesgo a esta comunidad indígena.

San Lorenzo de Azqueltán, en Jalisco, es una comunidad Wixárika y Tepehuana que desde hace diez años lucha por el reconocimiento de su territorio ancestral y contra el despojo que pretenden realizar pequeños propietarios y ejidatarios de la zona. En los años que llevan defendiendo su territorio, han sufrido una serie de agresiones escaladas que han llegado a arrebatarle la vida a personas de la comunidad. En los últimos días, el despojo y el hostigamiento se han hecho presentes de nuevo en el territorio.

A través de un comunicado difundido por el Congreso Nacional Indígena, el pasado 26 de junio la comunidad denunció que recientemente se ha vivido un clima de máxima tensión, así como una serie de amenazas en su contra que han ido escalando.

En primer lugar, la comunidad denuncia que desde los primeros días de junio, un policía municipal de Villa Guerrero de nombre Efraín Reyes, presuntamente por orden de ejidatarios, colocó una puerta obstruyendo el paso del camino que conduce a un pozo de agua conocido como El Tacuache, el cual representa la única fuente de agua para consumo humano de la comunidad de Azqueltán. Los comuneros señalan que esta acción arbitraria vulnera sus derechos humanos y les despoja de un bien común que forma parte de sus tierras comunales.

De acuerdo a Quetzal Prado, abogada de la comunidad, el pozo El Tacuache se encuentra a escasos diez metros del río Bolaños, por lo que la acción de bloquear el acceso a él, además de ser un despojo para la comunidad, representa una violación a la Ley Nacional de Aguas.

Por otro lado, en días pasados se llevo a cabo una reunión donde participaron autoridades del estado de Jalisco, así como representantes de la comunidad de Azqueltán y ejidatarios opositores a la comunidad, con el objetivo de establecer acuerdos para evitar confrontaciones en el territorio en disputa. Sin embargo, en su comunicado la comunidad señala que al día siguiente de esta reunión, un grupo de personas, encabezadas por Fabián Reyes Márquez, acudieron a un predio comunal llamado La Peña Blanca, el cual históricamente ha pertenecido la comunidad de Azqueltán, para intentar tomar posesión de él.

En el predio se encontraban trabajando comuneros Wixaritari y Tepehuanos de la comunidad, a quienes el grupo invasor amenazó con llevarlos a la cárcel, bajo el argumento de que al tomar posesión del predio, estaban siguiendo indicaciones de la Dirección de Asuntos Agrarios del Gobierno del Estado de Jalisco. De esta manera, las personas agresoras amenazaron a los comuneros con que llamarían a la policía para que los “levantaran”. Días más tarde este mismo grupo de personas volvió a ingresar al predio, donde retiró los postes y el alambrado colocado por comuneros de Azqueltán, y se llevó dichos materiales.

En su comunicado, la comunidad de Azqueltán responsabilizó al gobierno de Jalisco por su falta de compromiso para detener y prevenir la violencia que continuamente amenaza a la comunidad; así como denunció a las instituciones gubernamentales por promover la confrontación y permitir la impunidad.

Es importante recordar que la violencia contra los comuneros de Azqueltán cobró la vida de su representante agrario, Marcos Aguilar Rojas, en noviembre del año pasado, asesinato cometido, de acuerdo al último comunicado de la comunidad, por el mismo grupo que hoy intenta apoderarse del predio La Peña Blanca. Así mismo, otros comuneros han sido violentados en el pasado, quedando con secuelas de por vida, como señalan los hallazgos de la Misión Civil de Observación convocada por la Red Nacional de Organismos Civiles de Derechos Humanos (Red TDT) realizada en mayo pasado.

Para Quetzal Prado, abogada de la comunidad, existe el riesgo latente de que las agresiones hacia la comunidad sigan escalando ante la inacción de las autoridades de Jalisco: “Lo que nos preocupa es que vaya a ir escalando nuevamente y que se sigan incrementando esas situaciones de provocación o de despojo, por lo que resulta necesario que las acciones del gobierno sean tendientes a castigar este actuar ilegal por parte de las personas del ejido”, señaló la abogada, en entrevista con Avispa Mídia.

Ante las nuevas agresiones, la comunidad exige el cese de todo intento de despojo, así como que el gobierno de Jalisco tome acciones inmediatas para frenar una posible escalada de violencia en su territorio. De igual manera, los comuneros demandan de que se retire inmediatamente la puerta que bloquea el acceso al pozo El Tacuache, así como respeto absoluto a su territorio comunal. Por último, en el comunicado, la comunidad exige justicia por asesinato del comunero Marcos Aguilar Rojas, y la reparación integral de los daños realizados en la última agresión.

El 26 de junio pasado, comuneros de Azqueltán recuperaron la posesión del predio invadido, donde continúan trabajando por acuerdo de su asamblea. En este contexto, la comunidad llama a las redes que les han acompañado, así como a la sociedad civil, a permanecer pendientes de los sucesos de los próximos días y a alzar la voz frente a los intentos de despojo de su territorio.

author: By Niko Georgiades, Unicorn Riot
title: Charged in Anti-ICE Conspiracy, Two Minnesota Defendants Speak Out
content:
Activists say they’re being targeted for their political beliefs by a retaliatory government seeking to quash dissent

Minneapolis, MN — As the last Prairieland defendants were sentenced to extreme lengths of prison time in Texas today, the latest victims of Trump’s NSPM-7 political targeting appeared in a federal court in Minneapolis. Fifteen community activists facing federal conspiracy charges for their activism during the government’s deadly Operation Metro Surge pled not guilty this afternoon during their arraignment.

“It’s about quelling dissent in Minneapolis,” said healthcare worker and activist Isaac Sant to Unicorn Riot a week after his home was raided. “And it’s about coming after the movement that rose up against ICE during Metro Surge in December and January.”

The 36-year-old Sant, listed at the top of the indictment, said the charges are “a naked attempt to silence our voices, to squash dissent and to have a chilling effect on organizing here in the Twin Cities.” Which Sant noted, is “not going to work.”

The 94-page indictment unsealed on June 16 describes many of the defendants as “anarchists” and “antifascists,” both labeled as “terror groups” in the most recent White House counterterrorism documents.

The charges are a continuation of Trump and Stephen Miller’s vindictive domestic policies as federal agencies are directed to go after political opponents using the NSPM-7 directive and an executive order designating antifa as a domestic terrorist organization — despite there being no formal classification of antifa as a terror org. Antifa is an ideology against fascism and is short for anti-fascist.

Federal Indictment on Minnesota 15 Peddles DOJ ‘Antifa’ Conspiracy Angle After Raids

“With regards to NSPM-7, just know that these cases are going to continue. And while we may be anarchists, please don’t think that it’s going to stop there,” said Sant’s housemate Cal Robinet, who’s also one of the 15 indicted.

Speaking to UR, Robinet, a 37-year-old union electrician and activist, noted the Niemöller poem, First They Came, and said what the government is calling antifa is actually a “boogeyman that doesn’t exist” and they’re using that to go “after anybody who says no to them.”

“When they say we’re coming for anti-fascists, what they’re calling Antifa is a boogeyman that doesn’t exist. What they’re doing is they’re going after anybody who says no to them. And you should not be surprised when that starts applying to you.”

Responding to the deadly and racially-biased immigration enforcement of 4,000 federal agents occupying the metro area during the winter — the largest mass deployment of federal agents ever to take part in an immigration operation — countless thousands of community members across the Twin Cities organized themselves to protect their neighbors.

“I think it’s really important to point out that the retaliation that we’re seeing from the federal government isn’t just related to our speech, it’s related to the power that we have together,” Robinet said.

Unicorn Riot coverage of ICE In Minnesota 2025-2026

Several of the indicted are trade unionists and educators, a fact Robinet was quick to highlight. “It’s no secret that a lot of the people that were targeted are union organizers who are being charged for some of their alleged actions on [Jan. 23, 2026], the day of no work, no school, no shopping.”

Robinet and Sant shared their experience being raided. Robinet recalled how a Homeland Security media team recorded the arrest and the perp-walk into custody. They both gave their opinions on the indictment and the Prairieland sentencing. They also thanked the community for the “inspiring” support they’ve received — see their full transcripts below and videos above.

Robinet and Sant are both charged with felony counts of conspiracy to impede or injure a federal officer. Sant is additionally charged with felony interstate stalking for allegedly observing federal agents going into Wisconsin from the Whipple Federal Building.

Magistrate Judge David T. Schultz is presiding over the case. The day the indictment was unsealed, the government filed a ‘complex case’ motion asserting that they had more than 20 terabytes of evidence and needed more time to prepare their prosecution and release their discovery.

Yesterday, a joint response was filed by the defendants noting that the prosecution didn’t cite “any legal authority” in its motion that sought to “avoid its discovery obligations for 90 days.” Today in court, the judge did not grant the government’s motion and ordered the prosecutors to meet with the defense by July 10 to come up with a plan on how to handle the discovery and to submit a proposal by July 17.

Droves of federal prosecutors in Minnesota have quit over the U.S. government’s improper handling of immigration cases this year. Judges have admonished federal investigators and prosecutors in many of the cases, including the non-immigration cases being brought against U.S. residents.

In this year’s first federal conspiracy indictment in Minnesota over the January protest of an ICE field director at Cities Church in St. Paul, prosecutors were able to get the complex case motion passed but along with the investigators, they’ve been scolded by the judge over their motions and warrants.

Additionally, last week federal prosecutors were dealt a blow as the first case against a community member for standing up for immigrants in this new wave of immigration enforcement fell apart. Artist and activist Isa Lopez had five federal charges with a possibility of eight years in prison reduced to one misdemeanor and was sentenced to time served and a $25 fine.

Today, one of the Minnesota 15 defendants filed a motion to amend the release conditions that were imposed on the group, particularly the order that they cannot contact each other — which doesn’t apply to Sant and Robinet, who live together. In the motion, defense attorney Jordan Kushner noted, “this case should be recognized as the federal government’s extension of its repressive conduct from invasive and brutal actions in the community to weaponization of the legal system against those who dissent.”

Operation Metro Surge ‘Brought Terror and Human Rights Violations to Minnesota Communities’

Federal Case Unravels, Four Felony Charges on Minnesota Activist Are Turned Into One Misdemeanor

Unsealed Court Docs Spotlight Judge’s Rejection of Federal Search Warrants in Cities Church Case

Trump Admin Targets Press and Activists in Minnesota, Indicts ‘The Righteous 39’

“My name’s Isaac. I’m a 36 year old healthcare worker and an activist living here in Saint Paul, Minnesota. I was one of 15 people indicted on conspiracy charges for activity related to protesting ICE. They broke down this door. They broke into our garage. They, they dragged Cal out of bed in their underwear, and they took three cell phones and a computer out of my room. And then an hour later, they came and got me at my girlfriend’s house in Minneapolis. And when I was over there, I knew they were coming before they were there, not only because they had already taken my roommates, but because I heard the sound of whistles and her neighbors were outside already following them.

And I just want to say, that’s exactly what these charges are about. It’s not about conspiracy to impede. It’s not about interstate stalking. It’s not about any of that. It’s about quelling dissent in Minneapolis. And it’s about coming after the movement that rose up against ICE during Metro Surge in December and January. If the things that I’m accused of doing are part of a criminal conspiracy, then 350,000 people who participated in the resistance here would also have to be part of that conspiracy. This is a naked attempt to silence our voices, to squash dissent and to have a chilling effect on organizing here in the Twin Cities. And I’m here to tell you, it’s not going to work. People in the community here are smart. They’re resilient. They have an indomitable will. And I have every faith that they’re going to keep fighting. This is an attempt by the government to drive a wedge in between good protesters and bad protesters, and try to shave off the radical flank of the movement and paint us like we’re different from everybody else. But we’re not. There’s nothing that we’re accused of doing that hundreds of thousands of people here in Twin Cities didn’t do when these jack booted thugs were kicking in our doors and kidnapping our immigrant neighbors, they took one of my coworkers from the gas station while she was pumping gas, a grandmother of three. And she’s still in detention in El Paso, Texas right now.

So my arraignment is going to be July 1st. I understand I’m going to go in there. I’m going to plead not guilty as a condition of my release. The judge put a no contact order on us, so I’m not allowed to talk to any of my co-defendants with the exception of Cal, because we’re housemates. So obviously I can’t be as involved as I would like in, in coordinating my own defense, as we’re only allowed to talk through our lawyers. Right now, we have a strong support committee. We have, you know, hundreds of people behind us who are supporting us and are doing work behind the scenes. My role right now is just to to keep my head up, to stay in solidarity with my co-defendants. I plan to refuse any plea deals that aren’t offered to everybody. This is not a normal criminal trial. This is a political case. This is political repression against organizers. And this is a case that’s going to be won in the political realm.

So the context for what’s happening to us here is that it’s happening at the same time as a, a national wave of political repression. All of these NSPM-7, and so-called Antifa cases, are a naked attempt to silence dissent and attack the regime’s political opponents. The FBI has been visiting people who are at Delaney Hall. We’ve got the Spokane Three case. Charges were recently dropped against the Broadview Six, but the ruling in the first NSPM-7 case, the Prairieland case in Dallas and Fort Worth, Texas. Judge Pittman there, I understand said out loud, ‘I am I’m giving all of you the the longest possible sentence to send a message to anyone else who might share your political beliefs,’ so they’re not even trying to dress it up as anything else. This is like naked, blatant political repression. We are living in an authoritarian country now.

Look, if you want to support us, the best thing you can do for me and my co-defendants, more so than protesting for us, moreso than donating money to our fundraiser, moreso than any of that, is just to keep doing what you’re doing. Stay out there, keep doing all the legal observing against ICE that is lawful and is effective and is the reason they’re cracking down on us in the first place. It’s to stop you from doing that. So I want you to get out there, keep doing what you’re doing. If we allow these charges to have their intended chilling effect, then ICE and Homeland Security will have won. And we can’t allow that to happen. We need our supporters to stay out there and stay active and keep documenting what these fascist psychopaths are doing in our streets.

I just want to say we’ve been really humbled and honored by the outpouring of support from the community. Our our fridge is, like, chock full right now because our neighbors keep keep delivering groceries here. There are people here fixing our door right now. But all of it has just been a reminder that that the the spirit animating the Twin Cities resistance has never been about radicalism. It’s always been about simple, everyday neighborliness. That’s why people resisted back during Metro Surge. And that’s why they’ve got our backs now. So to all of them, thank you.”

“Hi, I’m Cal. I’m 37. I’m a union low voltage electrician. I’m one of the organizers that was caught up in this unjust roundup of 15 people who are doing their best to protect their communities from the federal occupation and Operation Metro Surge. It’s no secret that a lot of the people that were targeted are union organizers who are being charged for some of their alleged actions on the day of no work, no school, no shopping. I think it’s really important to point out that the retaliation that we’re seeing from the federal government isn’t just related to our speech, it’s related to the power that we have together.

It’s one of those things that it’s so inspiring to see, and it’s something that we’re continuing to see with people supporting us after the horrific raid. So, I was asleep at six in the morning. I heard a crash, and then I heard some yelling. I thought it was just a cat that had knocked over a glass or something and someone yelled, but the yelling kept happening. So I walk out to my front door where it comes from, and then I hear, this is the raid get on the floor. And I see several people with assault rifles, suppressors, helmets, body armor, full military gear, all pointing guns at my head. So I get on the ground, they cuff me and they tell me to walk over to them across the broken glass. I told them I can’t walk across that broken glass, so they throw me a pair of slippers that aren’t mine.

And at that moment, I see the Homeland Security media crew. So they had a media crew there filming me half naked, trying to make their little anti-antifa video. One disgusting little creep just zooming in on me, zooming in on the violence. They opened up every container in my house, threw some stuff on the floor. They messed with my partner’s lingerie. You all know this is a house of trans refuge. And they targeted this house specifically because transgender people are a designated enemy of the state right now. And the way that they mess with my partner’s lingerie was disgusting. The way that they held my young roommates at gunpoint is disgusting. The way that they dragged me out in the rain in my underwear was disgusting. They sent helicopters after me. I had only heard one, but I heard one of the agents say that there were two.

Eventually they threw me some clothes and told me that I was being charged with federal conspiracy to impede. They brought me to jail and again, film crew perp walking me the whole time. I noticed a bunch of other people in jail that I’m familiar with. And not going to lie. Spending some time in a cell with your good friends could be a worse day. You know, there was singing, there was jokes, there was laughing. Keeping your spirits up is really important in a time like this, you know, not just for the defendants, but for everyone around you. These charges are a joke. There’s nothing that we’ve done that you know, thousands upon thousands of people haven’t done as well. These are all lawfully protected activities. And the reason that they’re throwing the book at us is because this is a political case to them. that we are enemies of state for our political beliefs, for activities as union organizers and for existing as queer people in this world.

So those of you may not be familiar. Prosecutor attempted to hold us in jail until the trial and the entire courtroom laughed at her, and she got extremely tilted. And the judge got very angry. But it just kind of goes to show you the level of absurdity of the charges that we’re facing. And the biggest thing that I think people need to keep in mind right now is that the reason they’re doing this is that they want you to be scared. Our tactics are working. They know it, and they’re on their back foot and they’re trying to make a big show of this. It’s the same reason they took all that footage of me, right? They’re trying to get me looking scared. And I’m not scared. I’m not scared of these charges. I’m not scared of these monsters. We can beat them. That’s why they’re acting this way. Let it be known that homosexuals are not cowards.

I think that more than anything, I want people right now to double down on their efforts. Double down on your mutual aid. Double down on your ICE watching. Double down on commuting. Double down on standing up for your neighbors. Keep those whistles on you. Keep calling people. Keep building friends. You know, the people that have been the most effective during this occupation are the people that have the most networks that they can tap into together.

You know, one of the most inspiring stories that I remember hearing is when ICE was trying to infiltratethe school pickup network so they could abduct children that are walking out of school. Is that the parents and teachers and the teachers union worked together to build the safety system for it, and some of the parents didn’t like the high vis vests. And so a knitting club got together to knit hats for all the all the Safe Watchers. And then a hacker club got together to tell all of these teachers what it looks like when somebody is trying to infiltrate your group, how to spot something like that. So all of these groups and networks coming together to make one big picture is what makes us the most safe. And that’s what I want to keep seeing from people. Always remember, you know, our revenge will be the laughter of our children. That means our immigrant children. That means our trans children. That means our refugee children. You know, those that don’t recognize that children belong to all of this are the worst monsters in this world. I think that the Prairieland sentence is something that the regime was able to push through in a favorable court, in a horrible situation that they’re going to try to use to intimidate. But Minnesota is not Prairieland. These bastards kicked a hornet’s nest, and they have no idea the lion that they’ve awakened.

With regards to NSPM-7, just know that these cases are going to continue. And while we may be anarchists, please don’t think that it’s going to stop there. You know that this is just a scapegoat to try and chip off one edge of the movement, much like that Niemöller poem. You know, first they came for X and then we came for Y. Know that that’s going on today, that when they say we’re coming for anti-fascists, what they’re calling Antifa is a boogeyman that doesn’t exist. What they’re doing is they’re going after anybody who says no to them. And you should not be surprised when that starts applying to you. It’s interesting to me that they put opposition to the U.S. government in part of the conspiracy, because to them, I could see why that would be a major crime. Because they want obedience at all costs. They love it. They just love that shit. But we’re free people. We’re free people, and we do as we please. And we love as we please, and we live as we please. You know, to live and love we must fight. And that’s the situation that we’re put in now. We’re standing up for any immigrant, any person of color or anyone who stands in their way, that’s who they’re coming after. And that’s who we need to be protecting right now.”

title: 13 июля — День рождения фигурантки «дела читинских анархистов» Любови Лизуновой
content:
Группа поддержки напоминает, что в апреле 2024 года Любе назначили 3,5 года колонии общего режима по делу о постах в телеграм-каналах «Шугань-25» и 75ZLO. В двух публикациях рассказывалось об антивоенных акциях прямого действия в Забайкалье. Изначально Любу судили еще и по статье о вандализме (из-за граффити «Смерть режиму» на окраине Читы), однако это дело против нее прекратили в связи с истечением срока давности.

Люба — первая в России несовершеннолетняя школьница, которую отправили в заключение за высказывания против российской агрессии в Украине. На момент задержания в 2022 году ей было 16 лет, она училась в десятом классе.

Сейчас Люба находится в ИК-7 в Улан-Удэ. Она работает на тяжелом швейном производстве старшей намеловщицей, но успевает заниматься творчеством: пишет стихи, рисует, поет. И даже организовала в ИК кружок йоги! До освобождения ей остается семь с половиной месяцев.

Люба недавно передавала группе поддержки, что у нее все хорошо, а одной из главных причин для этого называла поддержку людей со всего мира. Когда-то, в самом начале своего заключения, она писала, что ей не приходили письма только из Антарктиды.

Адрес для открыток и «бумажных» поздравлений: 670000, РФ, г. Улан-Удэ, ул. Пристанская, 4а, ИК-7, Лизуновой Любови Витальевне, 2006 г. р. Электронные письма можно отправить через сервис ZT (доступна оплата не только российскими, но и иностранными картами).

Любе и ее родителям также можно помочь финансово: группа поддержки ведет сбор на передачи на платформе «Заодно».

Тема вождизма, "фюрерства" в левых организациях — краеугольный камень при формировании любой системной или внесистемной политической структуры. Ведь с уходом лидер_а/ов, как правило, распадается вся организация, если не поддерживается при этом "извне".

То же верно и для правых, но с...

Так, в апреле 2026 года можно отметить высказывания, которые говорят о сближении позиций...

В еженедельной программе независимого русскоязычного радиоканала финский анархист Антти Раутиайнен рассказал о своём движении, о недавней первомайской демонстрации в Хельсинки, а также затронул ближневосточные проблемы и тему войны в Украине с точки зрения теории и практики анархизма.

author: David Swanson
title: The Pentagon’s Budget Redirected Would Exceed Our Wildest Dreams
content:
By David Swanson, World BEYOND War, July 1, 2026

Legacy “news” outlets have declared a national disaster emergency. It seems that we the people of the United States may be in imminent danger of having about 10% of the U.S. Congress give a damn about us, and — what’s worse — perhaps 5% give a damn about the other 96% of humanity too.

The panic seems misplaced, not only because Uncle Sam’s Oligarchs have still got 90% of our court jesters, the one emperor, and a majority of the Supremes, but also because the proposals for preschools, grocery stores, buses, and so forth hardly scratch the surface of the enormous pile of money dumped each and every year into a single criminal enterpr – er, I mean, government program. The actual cost of the U.S. military budget that Trump is asking for is $3 trillion. The point I am making here still works if you can’t be bothered with new facts and want to claim that the proposed military budget is half of that, but I think going with the most accurate facts we can find is always the best policy.

For some $3.7 trillion a year, the United States could have something that every other country in the World Cup has: healthcare as a human right free to all. That is, with only $0.7 trillion in new revenue each year (or the cost of a fairly mediocre war), everybody paying for health insurance could stop, everybody without health coverage could have it, and preventive care could begin to take over from emergency care. I don’t know how to calculate all the hours reclaimed from dealing with health insurance forms and so forth. But this would be a transformation of the U.S. government from principally a killing machine to principally a healthcare provider. Let’s look at some smaller proposals.

We could make college free for $75 billion a year, preschool for $35 billion, provide housing to everyone who lacks it for $29 billion a year. See those first three teeny tiny orange bars in the chart above. Can you image having those unbelievable things and still only be scratching the surface?

We could hire 100,000 people at $100,000 a year to work on what’s needed most. Total cost: $10 billion. We could end hunger on Earth for $93 billion a year. We could provide solar power to every house in the United States over 10 years for $120 billion each year. We could build 1,000 miles of high-speed rail each year for perhaps (depending how efficiently and where it’s done, of course) $200 billion. Or double or triple that for more efficiencies. It’s not as if we’re running our of money.

We could do all of these things, exceeding the wildest nightmares of Republicans and corporate Democrats alike, and still maintain absolute faith in militarism. We’d only have to assume that the United States was remotely like the rest of the world, which spends a tiny fraction of what the United States does on war machinery. Or we could grow more enlightened than that and go a lot further. The process would, by stages, enlighten us in any case. Regardless, we would need to invest something in the transition to peaceful industries, and to compensate, assist, and retrain anyone wanting such measures. Just to ridiculously over-invest in that concern, let’s chalk up another $200 billion.

Now, the things one can do for safety while disarming are many and include ceasing to supply the world with weapons, as well as making disarmament agreements, providing disarmament incentives, and supporting the rule of law, cooperation, investment in unarmed civilian defense, truth and reconciliation commissions, and so on. One thing on that list is actual aid — not military “aid” but actual, no-strings, support for human and environmental needs. I think a healthy quarter trillion on that each year would produce rallies around the world celebrating the United States instead of burning its flag.

Even then, we’d be only a bit over $1 trillion total. We could think a little harder about what’s needed most. Or we could send a check for $5,696 to every person in the United States and call it a good day’s work. We’ve not, of course, counted here the widely understood economic advantages of spending money in these ways rather than on wars — but everyone would share in those benefits too.

author: Sarah van Gelder
title: Finding real national pride on America’s 250th birthday
content:
During this year of celebrating our nation’s 250th anniversary, I’ve been experiencing an unexpected emotion: pride.

For months, it’s been something far different — a mixture of disappointment, disbelief and disgust at the undermining of our freedoms, our wellbeing, our children’s futures and even our prospects for survival.

But recently, something shifted for me. I saw the excitement and global unity of World Cup fans. I talked to small business owners here in my small town in Washington state who were placing signs in their windows to let immigrants know they are welcome. I saw my community come together to march and rally on Juneteenth, with speakers reminding us that all people deserve freedom — and that we still have work to do to achieve that founding aspiration of our nation. I watched gay and straight neighbors at a joyful and defiant Pride parade in Seattle.

So many people are choosing courage and freedom for all, doing the risky, heroic work of resisting a would-be dictator and his sycophantic henchmen. I am feeling more confident that the courage and strength of the American people will get us through this period of darkness — but only if we reckon honestly with how we got here.

We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.

That means doing exactly the work the Trump regime is working so desperately to prevent: coming to terms with our nation’s history of race-based violence, exclusion and displacement, beginning with the killing, land grabs and cultural suppression of the Indigenous peoples who were the original caretakers of this continent, and continuing with the cruel enslavement of people whose forced labor built the nation’s wealth.

The work we need to do is more than an anti-bias workshop. It is the deeper and long-overdue work our nation and institutions need. Instead of papering over inconvenient history and its continued harm, we can do the work that begins with the truth, allows healing, strengthens a culture of integrity and builds the solidarity needed to face the enormous challenges before us.

The conviction that this work is necessary led me to create a free zine, “Community Reckoning,” that offers a process for reckoning with our history. We don’t need to wait for leadership from Washington, D.C. to take on this challenge. We can start now in our communities, congregations, universities, civic groups and other organizations. “Community Reckoning” offers a path to doing this work together.

The framework is simple: Stop the harm. Tell the truth. Acknowledge. Repair. The STAR acronym echoes the North Star that guided enslaved people escaping bondage.

This framework grew out of lived experience when I co-led, along with an Indigenous tribal elder, a community group formed after the 2001 desecration of Suquamish Chief Seattle’s grave. Over several years, Native and non-Native residents countered the political influence of a property owners’ group that had been actively hostile toward the Suquamish Tribe (Stop the Harm). We learned and shared the tribe’s history (Tell the Truth). We acknowledged the harms done when tribal land was taken and the tribe’s very existence was under assault, and celebrated those working to improve relationships between the Native and non-Native communities  (Acknowledge). Finally, working alongside the tribal government, we helped win the return of land that had once been the center of the tribe’s village, where Chief Seattle had lived most of his life (Repair). The trust and transformation that resulted from this collaboration rippled outward for years.

The STAR path can also be seen in Georgetown University’s reckoning with the 1838 sale of more than 270 enslaved people to pay the university’s debts. Students and alumni who researched this history discovered that — contrary to the story the university had told — thousands of descendants of these families were still alive. Apologies followed: Rev. Timothy Kesicki, S.J., said, “The Society of Jesus which helped to establish Georgetown University and whose leaders enslaved and mercilessly sold your ancestors, stands before you to say that we have greatly sinned. … We are profoundly sorry.” Former President of Georgetown John J. DeGioia said, “Slavery remains the original evil of our Republic — an evil that our university was complicit in.”

The students persuaded the administration to rename two university buildings that had been named for the Jesuit leaders who arranged for this sale, and assessed themselves a fee in honor of those whose lives financed the institution’s existence.

The Jesuit order has donated and raised funds for a Descendants Truth & Reconciliation Foundation, which is now giving $10,000 scholarships to descendants, supporting modest home improvements to allow aged descendants to remain at home and sponsoring educational events and dialogues on racial justice.

These stories and others, along with practical tools, resources and inspiration from wise leaders, are contained in the zine.

The zine is built around practical ways communities can begin this work: learning local history, acknowledging harms, preventing ongoing injustice and working toward meaningful repair. Every community’s path will be different. But every community has one, and the integrity and deepened relationships that result are well worth the hard work.

Some people say we should put this reckoning off yet again — that there are more urgent matters as we face an authoritarian regime committed to entrenching its power, and other existential crises.

But we will only achieve sustainable progress when we heal our nation’s foundational wounds — a process that can’t wait for some ideal future.

For centuries, politicians and economic elites have used racial resentment to prevent working people of different backgrounds from joining together to win real improvements. They’ve turned natural allies into rivals while they consolidate power and ever-larger shares of our nation’s wealth.

The result is an increasingly powerful group of the ultra-rich supporting the right-wing surge in the United States and elsewhere. People of every race — but especially people of color — struggle to afford housing, education, health care, gas and even food, things most people in wealthy countries take for granted. Politicians answer to big money and to the lobbyists who flood the centers of power. The monied interests get their way, not us.

If we’re going to build power, we can only build it on a foundation of solidarity. And solidarity is only possible in movements that are fully inclusive — and have done the work of racial reckoning. Without it, internal fault lines caused by unaddressed trauma, unrecognized privilege and unintended harms will continue to undermine trust.

True reckoning means we don’t wait for a fracture. The burden doesn’t fall on people of color to identify the flaws or the injuries of institutions that have yet to reckon with their own history, biases and privilege. Instead, we collectively take on the needed work.

The benefits of this work go even further — they include the possibility of profound healing for all of us. Instead of accepting lies and half-truths, we build a foundation based on honest reckoning and the integrity that comes from insisting on the truth.

A person, an institution or a nation that papers over a traumatic and unresolved story doesn’t make it go away. The consequences of the falseness keep showing up.

We might prefer to tell ourselves we’re the greatest country on earth, the most free, the most exceptional; we might not want to think about what that greatness was built on.

Maybe what looks like American confidence — the swagger, the entitlement, the insistence that we have nothing to apologize for — is really a brittle facade. It’s what shame looks like when it doesn’t get named.

A university, a denomination, a nation that hasn’t told the truth about its own past has to keep defending a story that doesn’t hold up — and that takes energy and vigilance, and sometimes results in anger at any who would challenge the facade.

Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!

The good news is that the alternative to living with half-truths isn’t shame. It’s something better than both swagger and shame. It’s integrity. A person, an institution or a nation that has told the truth about its own history no longer needs to defend a false story. It can simply stand on what’s true. That’s a sturdier foundation than any myth.

Our history has been one of atrocities — and extraordinary courage. An honest accounting of our nation’s founding injustices gives us the opportunity to make them right. When we do, we won’t need the swagger anymore, because we’ll have something sturdier: the real thing. We can be unified in pride for this country, and unstoppable in coming together to build what could truly be a more perfect union.

The zine, “Community Reckoning” is free to download, print and share here.

Sarah van Gelder is the founding editor of YES! Magazine, a writer, public speaker, and community activist. She is also vice-chair of Free Speech TV and creator of two zines: "Community As Strategy" and "Community Reckoning," both available on her Substack: How We Rise.

Dear Sarah,  this work is so brilliant!   Thank you for the clarity and strength you continually demonstrate in putting integrity first!   I would be so pleased to offer my retreat center, Wellspring, if it can serve the cause with a gathering of folks for this work.

author: David Swanson
title: Submission by Australians for War Powers Reform to the National AUKUS Public Inquiry
content:
By Australians for War Powers Reform, July 1, 2026

Australians for War Powers Reform (AWPR) is a civil society organisation whose membership includes a wide range of qualifications and experience. We have since 2015 advocated for greater transparency and accountability from the federal government in its decisions for deployment of Australian forces to overseas wars. Since the government’s announcement of the AUKUS project in 2021, AWPR has concentrated on seeking details about it and assessing its implications. We welcome the initiative of the Australian Peace and Security Forum in establishing a community-based, independent inquiry and offer our submission below in response to its terms of reference.

AWPR has already made a submission to the inquiry by the Defence Subcommittee of the Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade into the Department of Defence Annual Report Parliamentary Inquiry (Defence Annual Report 2023–24). Its focus areas were Sovereign Defence Industrial Priorities: Evaluating the workforce and infrastructure required to build and maintain the submarines in Australia, Defence Estate & Security: Assessing the development of naval bases (such as HMAS Stirling in WA and infrastructure in Port Kembla/Adelaide), nuclear stewardship frameworks, and Uncrewed/Autonomous Systems: Examining the integration of Pillar II autonomous systems into the broader Australian Joint Force.

This inquiry into AUKUS is four years overdue. It should have been held as soon as the agreement was announced, if not by the Coalition government, then by the ALP. There was no urgency to justify giving the then Opposition 24 hours notice to agree to it, and there is none now. While the US and UK governments have both held inquiries into AUKUS, Australia has not. Such an inquiry could have acted to ensure that Australia respects and complies with the deeply-held rejection of nuclear weapons by our Pacific neighbours – by insisting that US (or UK) nuclear weapons are never brought into our territory. Instead, we have the likely prospect of US Virginia-class submarines at HMAS Stirling being equipped with new nuclear cruise missiles from the early 2030s.

An inquiry would also have considered the escalated risk of nuclear proliferation in the region, which Australia is committed to oppose as a signatory of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), signed in February 1970 and ratified in 1973. Under the NPT, Australia is recognized as a non-nuclear-weapon state and has committed to never acquire, manufacture, or receive nuclear weapons. Despite repeated assurances that Australia’s AUKUS submarines will not be nuclear-armed, their use of highly-enriched uranium fuel – which can also be used to fuel nuclear weapons – is a provocation to other nations to consider the same pathway for submarine propulsion.

Such an inquiry would have found that expanding the US military presence in Australia, including naval, air force and Marine deployments, far from making Australia safer from foreign attack, instead makes Australia a surrogate target for an attack on America and therefore less secure. Australia could become a proxy fighter in a war between the US and China, with disastrous results.

Such an inquiry would have sought the facts about China’s intentions in our shared region, and queried the basis of successive fluctuations in Australian perceptions of China as an economic partner and as an enemy. It would have revealed the disproportionate influence on Australian policy-makers of the US-dominated intelligence that informs the ‘Five Eyes’. It would have recognised that American aspirations for global hegemony are doomed, and that it is in Australia’s interests to improve relations with China by non-military means, accommodating it as many of our Indo-Pacific neighbours seek to do.

The Australian Submarine Agency states that the primary purpose of Australian submarines (and their interoperability with US submarines) is to protect vital trade routes. Given that most of our vital trade in the Pacific is with the nation that we are spending a fortune to protect ourselves from, the objectives of the AUKUS agreement are highly contestable.

Furthermore, the US military has been unable to protect the vital trade route of the Strait of Hormuz, demonstrating yet again that Australia has no influence over – but suffers the consequences of – such US political and strategic miscalculations.

An inquiry now would question the inability of the US to protect or to utilise its bases in its allied Middle Eastern nations in their current war with Iran. Australia has agreed to join Pacific nations including Guam, Japan and the Philippines in a US-led confrontation with China, with no Parliamentary debate or public consultation. This places Australia in a position where Australian military assets could be used in conflicts that are contrary to our interests and furthermore put Australian infrastructure and indeed the Australian population at great risk. The US Middle East allies were all first strike targets for Iranian retaliation in the recent conflict in the Gulf region.

Two fundamental questions therefore face Australia: they concern ANZUS and AUKUS. The 1951 ANZUS Treaty commits Australia and the US to do nothing more than to consult in accordance with our Constitutional processes in the event of an attack on either party in the Pacific area. The AUKUS agreement, however, commits Australia in effect to subsidising the US and UK nuclear submarine industries with no escape clause, although they can terminate it with a year’s notice. By locking Australia into our allies’ hostile intentions towards China, the AUKUS agreement clearly endanger Australia more than it protects us, and ANZUS doesn’t protect us from being drawn into a unilateral US action in the region, as happened in the Vietnam War in 1965

The Australian Commonwealth Government has military asset procurement rules including an assessment of the risk of the project failing during its lifetime. That neither the US nor the UK have the capacity to meet their own submarine construction needs should have been a red flag at the time the AUKUS agreement was entered into and yet this was not disclosed to the Australian public or to the Australian Parliament.

The quoted cost of AUKUS, like all defence contracts, can be expected to rise significantly over the life of the program, if it continues. The capacity of suppliers of submarines to the US and UK is already stretched, and Australia has no guarantee from either that what we are paying for will ever be delivered, nor that Australia will be compensated if it is not.

Australia is already investing heavily to build facilities for submarines in Western Australia and South Australia. With no experience of nuclear power and limited access to expertise in modern submarine technology, the likelihood of distortions in the labour market is obvious. If the project is abandoned, further workforce disruptions are likely. The same could apply if an east coast submarine base is built at Port Kembla or Newcastle.

Claims about job creation in all these ports are irrational: the same money could be spent on developing more skilled labour to meet existing shortages for peaceful purposes, not for building offensive weapons. The balance could be spent on cheaper, more appropriate non-nuclear submarines.

Australia is currently experiencing a shortage of infrastructure workers that is predicted to blow out to 300,000 by mid-2030. Australia currently has an unemployment rate of 4.5%, which is rising. Australia also has a severe housing construction shortfall, needing 116,000 by 2030. Where are the workers for all the promised jobs in the construction and extension of military bases and the accommodation of US personnel coming from and how does this
effect Australia’s housing crisis?

None of the AUKUS partners has the capacity to store nuclear waste safely for the hundreds of thousands of years (in the case of high-level waste) in which it should be isolated from the biosphere. The waste includes not only spent fuel, but decommissioned equipment and contaminated material. Experience in the US at Yucca Mountain and elsewhere, and in the UK at Sellafield, shows how intractable this problem is. Australia should not add to the radioactivity still present after the British nuclear tests at the Maralinga site. A high-level nuclear waste facility is a dangerous ambition which should not be considered, and yet that’s exactly what we’re committed to with nuclear-powered submarines.

Remote sites proposed for waste disposal are likely to be on Commonwealth and indigenous land. Transportation of waste is hazardous and would be likely to cover long distances, increasing the danger of accidental release.

Concern about the proposed nuclear submarine bases has been expressed by communities in the four proposed locations – Rockingham, Osborne, Port Kembla and Newcastle. We urge the Inquiry to recognise that ecological concerns are widespread in Australia about damage to humans and wildlife, and air, land and marine environments. Public resistance to bases is likely to divide communities and heighten disaffection with governments, both Federal and State. Opposition to AUKUS is creating hostility to foreign forces in Australia and is focussing on the US alliance.

A potential rise in CO2 emissions as a result of AUKUS activities should be quantified and taken into account as a negative factor. Defence operations are notorious polluters – including with PFAS – and Australia should be prepared to impose more rigorous controls on them than it has so far done.

In Earth’s Greatest Enemy, her 2026 film, American Abby Martin shows the extent of toxic chemical contamination of water, air and soil around US military sites. She also documents the common US military practice of incinerating unwanted munitions and equipment, and of discarding naval garbage at sea. She cites quotas in the thousands of large marine species that are allowed for US naval ‘target practice’. If this is what the US military does in its own territory, we cannot expect them to be more careful about trashing Australia’s environment. Will Australian governments stop them?

Defence contracts are often justified by claims that the skills and employment opportunities they will provide will flow on to create economic growth. As argued above, Federal and State governments can do this for less than the cost of AUKUS by increasing funding for training and infrastructure programs, and having more left for climate action, housing, health, education and even for Australia’s Future Fund.

The 2007 UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (Article 29) states that such people must have ‘free, prior, and informed consent’ over storage of hazardous materials on their lands.

Australian sovereignty, so often cited by Ministers as being strengthened by AUKUS, will instead be reduced by US command and control of the project. This is an intangible but fundamental consequence of the agreement, and one for which government must be held to account.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Tenaris Siat despidió a 150 operarios en la planta de Valentín Alsina: la respuesta de los trabajadores
content:
Allí se producen tubos con costura para la industria del gas. La empresa de Paolo Rocca decidió no renovar el contrato de casi la mitad de la planta aduciendo una baja en la producción.

La empresa Tenaris Siat del grupo Techint despidió a 150 trabajadores de la planta que tiene en Valentín Alsina. La empresa, propiedad de Paolo Rocca, decidió no renovar 150 contratos desde este 1° de julio aduciendo una baja en la actividad tras perder dos licitaciones de provisión de tubos para la construcción de gasoductos.

Los trabajadores de la empresa rechazaron la decisión empresarial en la cual fueron despedidos casi el 50% de una planta que cuenta en la cual hay 340 operarios. La misma llegó a tener 550 trabajadores en 2023 cuando allí se fabricaron los tubos para el Gasoducto Néstor Kirchner inaugurado en 2023 en una obra realizada en tiempo récord.

José Villa, delegado por la UOM en la fábrica, expresó en Radio Gráfica: “Queremos que la empresa abra un canal de diálogo y mantener la continuidad de los puestos de trabajo y la dignidad de los trabajadores porque, además buscan implementar la Reforma Laboral con los que quedan”.

Villa contó que los trabajadores realizaron el viernes un asamblea durante más de tres horas y que han recibido el apoyo de la Seccional Avellaneda de la UOM y de la conducción nacional con la presencia de Abel Furlán. Una conducción que recientemente fue desplazada por una intervención dispuesta por el Poder Judicial a pocas semanas de producirse el Congreso donde se renovaron autoridades.

“Le planteamos a la empresa mantener al personal por los próximos seis meses con un esquema de suspensiones. Son trabajadores altamente calificados de la cual no se pueden desprender por situaciones puntuales de corto plazo”, agregó.

Dylan Paz, también delegada por la UOM en la planta, detalló: “la empresa ya venía aplicando la reforma laboral sin la ley sancionada. Estos 150 compañeros que quedarían cesanteados son compañeros que están con un contrato de trabajo desde hace cuatro años, que lo vienen renovando mes a mes con la excusa de que no hay proyectos”.

“Así como avanzan con estos 150 despidos, desde el miércoles lo van a hacer con la organización sindical dentro de la planta”, sumó.

Tenaris Siat fue creada en 1948 para la provisión de tubos con una distribución de gas en expansión durante el primer gobierno de Juan Domingo Perón. “Desde 1948 es la primera vez que se utiliza un tubo que no sale de esta fábrica en la construcción de un gasoducto. Perteneció inicialmente al grupo Siam Di Tella, en los 70 pasa a manos del Estado nacional y en el 1986 de Techint. Fue creada y sostenida como parte de un proyecto de defensa y protección de la industria nacional”, contó Villa.

“La empresa tiene espalda para sostener los puestos de trabajo, le decimos a Paolo Rocca que no somos descartables. La planta tiene trabajo y está produciendo, lo que dicen es que no lo hace en forma suficiente para mantener a toda la planta. Se está produciendo tubería chica relacionada con el boom de Vaca Muerta”, agregó.

Por último, expresó: “Si la fábrica hoy no está funcionando al nivel que el Gobierno quisiera es por la decisión política de Paolo Rocca de apoyar a este gobierno, que se haga carga y que no despida a los trabajadores“.

Techint perdió la licitación a comienzos de año la licitación para la provisión de caños del gasoducto de 500 kilómetros de extensión que unirá Vaca Muerta con las costas de Río Negro a manos de la empresa de origen indio Welspum.
