The proclamation is Trump’s latest attempt to dismantle conservation guardrails for industrial fishing. Last April, the president signed a proclamation to open over 400,000 square miles of the Pacific Islands Heritage Marine National Monument to commercial fishing. He also issued an executive order intended to boost domestic seafood production, and his administration has continued to increase several fishery quotas. Then, this February, Trump signed another proclamation removing commercial fishing from the prohibited activities in two national monuments in the Atlantic.

“AMERICA FIRST FISHING POLICY,” the White House posted on Facebook after this month’s proclamation. “MASSIVE WIN FOR AMERICA’S FISHERMEN!” During the signing in the Oval Office, Trump himself promised the move would generate “millions and millions of dollars in new business for our great, really great fishermen” and lower seafood costs.

Congresswoman Kimberlyn King-Hinds, the sole congressional representative from the CNMI, attended the signing and said in a press release that she hopes the federal government will work with local officials and communities to implement the directive and that it creates jobs. “For the CNMI, ocean policy is local policy,” she said. “If American fishing activity grows in these waters, our goal should be to connect that activity to local jobs, local businesses, port activity, seafood infrastructure, and long-term food security for the Commonwealth.”

Numerous commercial fishers and groups have also hailed the president’s move to roll back the restrictions in areas such as Papahānaumokuākea. “We need to eat fish caught by our fishermen who follow U.S. laws,” Kitty Simonds, executive director of the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council, told Grist. Eric Kingma, executive director of the Hawai‘i Longliners Association, told Honolulu Civil Beat that he welcomed a review from the federal government “guided by sound science” on the scientific, economic, and cultural significance of the area, as well as management decisions that support “the long-term viability of Hawai‘i’s longline fleet.” After Trump signed the first commercial fishing proclamation last April, Kingma argued that ocean conservation and commercial fisheries can be compatible. “What we like about opening these up is the opportunity to fish there when the fish are there,” Kingma said at the time.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

But the administration’s strategy for boosting America’s $319 billion-dollar fishing sector has been riddled with unresolved legal questions.

In spring of last year, just days after the president’s April 2025 proclamation, the National Marine Fisheries Service, known as NOAA Fisheries, announced in a letter to fishing permit holders it had reopened commercial fishing in the Pacific Islands Heritage Marine National Monument. That ban was lifted for nearly four months, until last August, when a federal district judge ruled, in a lawsuit filed by the nonprofit law firm Earthjustice, that the move violated the federal rulemaking process.

Earthjustice attorney David Henkin believes that the lawsuit, which he led, may have prompted the administration to change its strategy for revising industrial fishing regulations. This shift became evident when, after the president’s Atlantic Ocean proclamation earlier this year, NOAA Fisheries went through the formal rulemaking process to change the regulation that previously banned commercial fishing in those monuments.

Still, there is another, more fundamental legal question that Henkin says remains open. Though Congress has absolute authority over the use and management of federal lands and waters, the Antiquities Act of 1906 also gave the president the authority to designate certain federal water and lands containing scientific, historic, or cultural resources as protected monuments. No federal court has yet ruled whether the Antiquities Act allows a president to undo a national monument or their protections, though several cases are pending. Earthjustice is again preparing to challenge the administration in court. “It’s anyone’s guess what these folks are going to do, other than play fast and loose with the law,” said Henkin.

Opening these areas to commercial fishing has the additional effect of edging out traditional Indigenous fishers, who not only tend to practice smaller-scale, more sustainable fishing, but are also largely exempt from the commercial fishing bans in protected waters. Indigenous fishers, for instance, still retained the right to subsistence fish under the protections Trump just stripped back within the Mariana Trench Marine National Monument. “If anyone gains to benefit from this, it’s not going to be the traditional Indigenous communities,” said Steven Mana‘oakamai Johnson, Kanaka Maoli from the island of Saipan and assistant professor at Cornell University. “It’s going to be businesses, corporations, and those who have these larger vessels.”

Even in American Samoa — where tuna is the biggest export and support for commercial fishing is widespread — some are questioning the expansiveness of Trump’s latest proclamation and its effect on Indigenous peoples. A year ago, congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata from American Samoa said of the Pacific marine monuments, “Neither presidents Bush, Obama, or Biden ever asked American Samoa what they wanted before they took away our Indigenous fishing rights without any science.” But now Amata is concerned about how fishing around Rose Atoll could also infringe on Indigenous rights. “Amata remains convinced that Rose Atoll should be off limits, her longstanding position, especially as she respects the cultural rights of the people of Manu‘a,” her office said in a press release.

Camilo Mora, a scientist at the University of Hawai‘i at Mānoa, challenges the administration’s argument that deregulation will create jobs and strengthen the fishing sector. Mora has long studied the relationship between biodiversity, fisheries, and the global food system, and argues any short-term economic benefits of the move will be offset by the long-term ecosystem losses. Most U.S. waters, in any case, are already open to commercial fishing — highly protected areas where all extractive activity is banned make up about 3 percent.

Papahānaumokuākea, for one example, is one of the largest marine protected areas in the world and is a refuge for rare and ecologically significant species. The Hawaiian monk seal, humpback whales, and green sea turtles are among the more than 7,000 species found there, many of which are critically endangered. Opening up the Mau and Ho‘omalu zones of the area to commercial fishing, Mora warns, could trigger a trophic cascade — when a change in the top predator’s population or behavior ripples throughout the food chain — that will then drive “all of these populations to collapse.”

“We are destroying the capacity of the oceans to make the food we need,” said Mora.

For Kikiloi in Hawai‘i, what’s at stake is not just food — it’s the ability for Indigenous people in Hawai‘i to stay connected to their ancestors. He’s not surprised that scientists like Mora have found some of the oldest living corals on Earth in Papahānaumokuākea, because Hawaiian oral histories describe it as the place where life began. “It’s the place where our souls return to after death,” he said. “It’s hard to exist as Hawaiians nowadays if every aspect of your environment is degraded.”

title: Informe del 13º Congreso de la IFA, 3-5 de abril de 2026, Atenas, Grecia
content:
El 13º Congreso de la Internacional de Federaciones Anarquistas (IFA-IAF) tuvo lugar en Atenas durante el fin de semana del 3 al 5 de abril de 2026, organizado por Αναρχική Πολιτική Οργάνωση – Ομοσπονδία Συλλογικοτήτων (Organización Política Anarquista-Federación de Colectivos - APO). Entre las demás federaciones que participaron se encontraban la Federazione Anarchica Italiana (FAIt, Italia), la Fédération Anarchiste (FA, francófona), la Federazione Anarchica Siciliana (FAS, Sicilia), la Federación Libertaria Argentina (FLA), la Federacija za anarhistično organiziranje (Federación para la Organización Anarquista, FAO, Eslovenia y Croacia), la Федерация на анархо-комунистите в България (FACB, Federación de Anarco-comunistas en Bulgaria), la Anarchist Federation (AF, Gran Bretaña), con invitados observadores individuales de Brasil (Aurora Negra y Terre Livre) y Serbia (Klasna Solidarnost). No participaron federaciones miembros y grupos asociados de México, Brasil, Checo-Eslovaquia, el Foro Anarquista de habla alemana y el Foro Anarquista Kurdo, este último debido a preocupaciones por la situación en Oriente Medio. También se invitó a compañeros cubanos, pero el contacto ha sido cada vez más difícil durante el bloqueo económico.

Para que la conferencia transcurriera sin problemas, el Congreso se celebró en un único lugar, la okupa Lelas Karagianni 37 (LK37), un impresionante bloque de apartamentos con larga trayectoria, la okupa más antigua de Grecia. El almuerzo y la cena fueron proporcionados por compañeros de la okupa y se puso a disposición de los visitantes algo de alojamiento. Se alquiló equipo de traducción para ofrecer traducción simultánea, aunque el idioma principal fue el inglés. La LK37 también fue la sede de una reunión pública titulada "La posición de los anarquistas sobre los conflictos militares y la amenaza de generalización de la guerra", el sábado por la noche, organizada por APO.

El Congreso de la IFA se celebra cada tres o cuatro años, y las reuniones de delegados intermedias (CRIFA) se utilizan para conectar a las federaciones y planificar agendas y actividades, así como para desarrollar documentos para el debate y la construcción de consensos. La toma de decisiones es ascendente, de modo que las federaciones proponen inicialmente temas para el orden del día y luego elaboran sus documentos y posiciones sobre esos temas para presentarlos al congreso. El congreso se estructuró con sesiones plenarias con todas las federaciones presentes, por ejemplo, sobre el tema de las perspectivas anarquistas sobre las insurrecciones mundiales (como el levantamiento en Irán, zonas del Mediterráneo, Madagascar, Indonesia y Nepal). Además, las federaciones participantes en el congreso co-organizaron una serie de talleres sobre los siguientes temas: Sudán, la extrema derecha, las luchas educativas, el medio ambiente, el patriarcado y la violencia de género, y el mundo digital (materiales en línea y ciberseguridad), y se debatieron algunos aspectos administrativos de la IFA.

La primera plenaria, "Contra el totalitarismo moderno del Estado, el Capitalismo y la Guerra", compartió perspectivas sobre el antimilitarismo. Los temas incluyeron la oposición a las bases aéreas o aviones de la OTAN (Italia, Sicilia, Creta) y a la expansión de la OTAN en Europa del Este, la reintroducción del servicio militar obligatorio (Croacia, Francia), la represión estatal de las actividades de solidaridad con Palestina (como la ley antiterrorista utilizada contra Palestine Action en el Reino Unido), y el aumento del gasto militar, incluidas inversiones de doble uso como la ampliación de aeropuertos, puertos marítimos o sistemas ferroviarios en los que los trabajadores podrían intervenir.

Aunque no siempre es posible alcanzar el consenso, el congreso logró avances significativos en varias cuestiones. En particular, las federaciones italiana y griega habían elaborado posiciones detalladas sobre las luchas de género con documentos aprobados por sus federaciones que aportaban perspectivas sobre la violencia de género sistémica (APO) y el transfeminismo (FAIt), por ejemplo, desde la FAI Italia: "El arraigo y la expansión de los movimientos transfeministas y queer es cada vez más indispensable frente a la intensificación de la opresión patriarcal en la fase actual, en la que, en varias partes del mundo, su vínculo con la opresión religiosa es cada vez más fuerte. En Italia, el gobierno de Meloni ha producido actos legislativos específicos de carácter patriarcal y familista para apoyar la tasa de natalidad dentro de la familia tradicional. Sin embargo, el familismo y la defensa de la familia tradicional, sexista y jerárquica, no son solo patrimonio de la derecha reaccionaria, porque también hay un familismo en la tradición de la izquierda". La FAIt también vinculó el aumento de la militarización con un incremento de la cultura machista.

APO se centró en la violencia patriarcal: "En un período en el que el totalitarismo moderno se moviliza para reprimir a los pueblos que se rebelan y aumentan las voces nacionalistas y fascistas, las mujeres, en todas partes del planeta, y especialmente las de los estratos plebeyos [clase trabajadora], se enfrentan, más allá del riesgo de muerte, desplazamiento, hambre y enfermedad, a la amenaza diaria de la violencia de género, la tortura sexual y las ejecuciones, como herramientas de conquista y sometimiento". APO destacó los ataques a los derechos al aborto en Estados Unidos y el uso sistemático de la violencia de género como arma de guerra en Sudán y Palestina, pero también, de manera similar a lo que ocurre en Italia, el recurso de los nacionalistas a la "naturaleza femenina" para reivindicar un papel de la maternidad en interés nacional.

El taller "Auge de la Extrema Derecha y Respuesta Antifascista" fue presentado por la AF y la FA. La AF utilizó el contexto del ascenso de Reform UK para debatir los aspectos culturales de las ideologías y actividades de extrema derecha. Hubo un gran interés en el uso de las leyes de orden público en Gran Bretaña para limitar la protesta. Si bien la detención preventiva mediante cargos de conspiración no es nueva en el Reino Unido, parece más difícil de justificar para el Estado en países donde ha habido un historial de dictadura o donde el antifascismo se menciona incluso como parte de la constitución. En Italia y Grecia, las raíces de las dictaduras fascistas son profundas. Pero culturalmente, temas fascistas como "Dios, Patria y Familia" están resurgiendo, y ahora los anarquistas y sus espacios están siendo específicamente atacados por la policía durante el liderazgo de extrema derecha de Meloni en Italia. Aunque la época dorada de Amanecer Dorado en Grecia es pasado, en parte debido a su represión por parte del Estado tras el asesinato de un cantante antifascista, los vínculos de sus miembros con la extrema derecha de "rostro amable" más mediática no han desaparecido.

Si bien en algunos países es posible apelar a la historia, en Brasil, Bulgaria y Serbia la amenaza de la violencia neonazi en la calle sigue siendo hoy un gran peligro, porque operan y se reúnen o organizan eventos abiertamente, además de atacar directamente y a veces asesinar a anarquistas en las calles. Los anarquistas, a su vez, han encontrado formas creativas de combatirlos, como fomentar clases masivas de defensa personal en los barrios, como en las comunidades de favelas de Brasil.

El taller sobre educación fue una oportunidad importante para comprender los cambios en Grecia, donde se están imponiendo modelos de colaboración privada en los institutos, y los docentes que resisten la privatización y el aumento del uso de la evaluación intensiva del alumnado en todos los rangos de edad están siendo victimizados. También existe una mayor amenaza para la organización anarquista en las universidades. Por lo tanto, la necesidad de sindicatos de base sólidos es de vital importancia. En el lado alentador, el Congreso tuvo conocimiento de un instituto gratuito, la Escuela Libre de Constitución (ELC) en Buenos Aires, Argentina, que tiene como objetivo utilizar métodos anarquistas de enseñanza con jóvenes de 16 a 18 años, y también del Laboratorio de Educación Anarquista (LEA) en São Paulo, Brasil, en el Centro de Cultura Social (CCS). La iniciativa LEA, llevada a cabo por la Biblioteca Terra Livre, tiene como objetivo estudiar, producir y experimentar con prácticas pedagógicas para niños, incluyendo su uso en ferias del libro anarquistas para facilitar la participación significativa de los niños en esos eventos.

La sesión de taller sobre "El expolio de la Naturaleza" fue presentada por APO y se centró en los problemas políticos, culturales y sociales en torno a la crisis climática y el expolio de la naturaleza y las comunidades locales por parte del Estado y el capital. La sesión incluyó el debate sobre las oposiciones populares a la extracción de recursos, el capitalismo "verde" y el control sobre la naturaleza y las comunidades locales. La sesión también abordó el aumento de la urbanización, la mercantilización y la gentrificación. Se establecieron fuertes vínculos con el antimilitarismo en relación con las protestas contra el desarrollo de infraestructuras. Se destacaron los problemas con la inversión de 1 billón de dólares de la "Agenda 2030" de la ONU para el cambio climático.

Al final del fin de semana, el 13º congreso de la IFA produjo una declaración conjunta titulada "Contra la Dictadura Global del Estado y el Capitalismo, contra la Guerra y el Fascismo", centrada en el antimilitarismo, vinculada a la sesión plenaria. También produjo una declaración de solidaridad con los anarquistas cubanos. Ambas serán ratificadas por las federaciones de la IFA antes de su publicación. Se escucharon grandes aplausos cuando Klasna Solidarnost (Serbia) anunció su intención de solicitar su adhesión a la IFA como grupo asociado (una condición que se utiliza para grupos que tienen la intención de crecer hasta convertirse en una federación). Se propuso una sede para el próximo congreso, mientras que la FA aceptó asumir el papel de Secretaría tras la buena labor de la FAO durante los últimos años. Se acordó un plan para celebrar otra reunión en el Mediterráneo, así como un próximo número de la revista de la IFA sobre perspectivas antimilitaristas, en el que las federaciones miembros de la IFA presentarán artículos. Tras el informativo taller sobre Sudán realizado por la FAS y la FA en el Congreso, se presentó un nuevo cartel de solidaridad, destacando las luchas anarquistas sudanesas. Tras el fin de semana, se celebró en Atenas una reunión de solidaridad con los migrantes sudaneses que ofreció a quienes se quedaron más tiempo la oportunidad de conocer mejor la situación. Los compañeros de la IFA también fueron invitados por la FAO a la próxima Feria del Libro Anarquista de los Balcanes en Skopie, Macedonia, en septiembre. El congreso concluyó con un ruidoso homenaje al compañero de la FA Jean-Marc Raynaud, fundador de Ediciones Libertarias y de la escuela anarquista "Bonne Aventure", fallecido a finales de marzo.

Publicado originalmente en el sitio web de la IFA, https://i-f-a.org/2026/04/14/report-from-the-13th-ifa-congress-3-5-april...">aquí.

author: gavroche
title: [Rojava] Informe de abril del nordeste de Siria
content:
Queridas compañeras: En primer lugar, queremos expresar nuestra autocrítica por nuestra ausencia las últimas semanas. Estamos reorganizando nuestro sistema de trabajo y no hemos podido enviar las actualizaciones a tiempo, ni comunicarlas. Así que, más vale tarde que nunca: a partir de ahora, retomaremos los informes mensualmente.

Se ha iniciado una campaña bajo el lema «Todas somos YPJ», que está ganando repercusión tanto a nivel nacional como internacional. El movimiento y las organizaciones de mujeres de Rojava iniciaron esta campaña el 26 de abril con el objetivo de que las YPJ formen parte del proceso de integración.

Como ya hemos mencionado, el papel de las YPJ y de las organizaciones de mujeres del noreste de Siria en general es y seguirá siendo un punto conflictivo en las negociaciones, ya que la lucha de las mujeres es un pilar fundamental de la revolución, mientras que al-Sharaa, con su ideología fundamentalista islámica, no quiere legitimar el poder de las mujeres ni el lugar que les corresponde en la sociedad.

Disturbios y represión bajo el gobierno del Gobierno de Transición de Siria (GTS)

El MIT apoya a fuerzas tribales árabes.
	Circulan informes sobre supuestas reuniones entre el MIT (servicio de inteligencia turco) y algunos líderes tribales para negociar y formar grupos capaces de perpetrar ataques y asesinatos en zonas de mayoría kurda del noreste de Siria. Presuntamente, el MIT proporciona armas, entrenamiento y financiación a hombres vinculados a lo que se ha presentado como "ejércitos tribales", creando una red clandestina capaz de llevar a cabo ataques insurgentes en regiones kurdas. Estos grupos podrían contar con el apoyo tácito del gobierno, permitiendo a las fuerzas gubernamentales negar cualquier vínculo oficial, basándose en las tácticas de contraguerrilla paramilitar que el Estado turco ha utilizado durante décadas contra el movimiento kurdo.

El mayor convoy de repatriados a Afrin
	Un quinto convoy de refugiados de Afrin partió de Haseke el 10 de mayo, con aproximadamente 1600 familias kurdas que se vieron obligadas a abandonar sus hogares en 2018 tras la operación militar Rama de Olivo. Este ha sido el mayor convoy hasta la fecha, superando al cuarto que partió a principios de mayo con alrededor de 1000 familias.

El primero de estos convoyes llegó a Afrin el 9 de marzo, con cerca de 400 familias desplazadas. Un segundo grupo de unas 200 familias llegó el 4 de abril, seguido de un tercer convoy de aproximadamente 800 familias que arribó a Afrin el 14 de abril. En total, se contabilizan alrededor de 4000 familias que han regresado a Afrin, aunque la situación allí aún es incierta, ya que la influencia del Estado turco y sus grupos armados, integrados por miembros del antiguo Ejército Nacional Somalí (ENS), siguen teniendo una fuerte presencia en la región.

Reorganización de los cargos de poder en el gobierno de Siria
	Ahmad al-Sharaa emitió una serie de decretos presidenciales que introducen nuevos nombramientos para altos cargos en la Presidencia y varios ministerios.

Según los decretos, Abdulrahman Badr al-Din al-A'ma fue nombrado Secretario General de la Presidencia, en sustitución de Maher al-Sharaa, hermano del presidente. Khaled Fawaz Zaarour sucedió a Hamza Mustafa como Ministro de Información. En el Ministerio de Agricultura, Bassel Hafez al-Suweidan fue nombrado ministro, en sustitución de Amjad Badr.

Los decretos también nombraron nuevos gobernadores en varias gobernaciones. Ghassan Elias al-Sayyed Ahmad fue nombrado gobernador de Quneitra, en sustitución de Ahmad al-Dalati; Murhaf Khaled al-Naasan, gobernador de Homs; Ahmad Ali Mustafa, gobernador de Latakia; y Ziyad Fawaz al-Ayesh, gobernador de Deir ez-Zor.

Estancamiento del proceso de paz en Bakur.
	En declaraciones recientes, los líderes del movimiento apoísta afirmaron que la iniciativa de paz con Turquía se encuentra prácticamente paralizada, dado que Ankara no ha implementado las reformas legales y políticas necesarias para impulsar el proceso.

La dirección del movimiento apoísta también ofreció una rueda de prensa para conmemorar este hecho.

La dirección del Movimiento Apoísta también ofreció una rueda de prensa con motivo del primer aniversario del congreso de disolución del PKK, donde evaluó los logros del movimiento de liberación kurdo. Destacaron que la disolución del PKK debe entenderse como un nuevo comienzo para el movimiento de liberación kurdo, abriendo espacio para el desarrollo político y democrático.

Evaluación
	En el último mes, hemos visto cómo las tensiones bélicas entre Estados Unidos e Israel contra Irán siguen proyectando su sombra sobre todo Oriente Medio. Las potencias occidentales formalizan sus lazos con el gobierno sirio, y hoy (11 de mayo) Siria y la UE celebrarán las primeras conversaciones políticas de alto nivel desde la caída del régimen de Assad. Se espera que las conversaciones se centren en establecer un marco político para las relaciones entre la UE y Siria y en evaluar el apoyo de la UE a la recuperación económica y la transición política.

El proyecto de la Administración Autónoma del Noreste de Siria como institución oficial está llegando a su fin, ya que las conversaciones sobre la integración en el Estado sirio se están convirtiendo en la realidad cotidiana del Noreste de Siria. El movimiento revolucionario trabaja para defender los valores y logros de la revolución mientras las instituciones formales se disuelven, pero las comunas y el movimiento popular continúan su camino. Muchos lamentan estas pérdidas, pero al mismo tiempo son muy conscientes de las razones que las motivaron.

Las decisiones de las FDS y la DAANES evitaron una masacre, y todos en el terreno son muy conscientes de ello. La vida de la población de NES se antepuso a cualquier agenda política, lo que permitió una relativa paz y calma. Los órganos políticos y militares de NES maniobraron de la mejor manera posible para evitar masacres o batallas largas y sangrientas. Mientras continúa el intercambio de prisioneros, las familias celebran el regreso de sus hijos e hijas a casa, sabiendo que en otras circunstancias no podrían volver a verlos jamás.

Al mismo tiempo, se han logrado importantes avances políticos para los kurdos en Siria, con el reconocimiento formal de sus derechos en la constitución y los decretos oficiales. Esto genera cierta esperanza de una lucha política en lugar de la simple continuación de la guerra, pero todos son conscientes de que esos acuerdos no significan nada si la población no está organizada y preparada para luchar cuando el Estado intente revocar cualquiera de esos logros. Los medios de autodefensa también se han preservado en cierta medida, asegurando que las FDS no se rindieran ni entregaran sus armas.

Hoy es evidente que al-Sharaa es un buen estratega. Jugó muy bien sus cartas para alcanzar la posición central que deseaba. Es un pragmático que no tiene reparos en comprometer las líneas ideológicas de su organización para fortalecer su control sobre el poder estatal sirio. Hasta qué punto intentará regresar a sus raíces islamistas a medida que consolida su poder, hasta qué punto adoptará la política capitalista occidental y desempeñará el papel de jefe de Estado responsable ante las potencias occidentales, es algo que se irá aclarando con el tiempo.

author: gavroche
title: [Madrid] Comunicado: En respuesta al comunicado emitido por Taberna Garibaldi
content:
Ante la pronta contestación a raíz del comunicado emitido por este Sindicato el pasado martes dieciséis de junio acerca de la situación en la Taberna Garibaldi, así como algunas de las afirmaciones esparcidas a tenor de ambas publicaciones, CNT Comarcal Sur expone lo siguiente:

El modelo sindical de este Sindicato y la Confederación en la que se organiza es el de la Sección Sindical. CNT rechaza participar de las elecciones y comités de empresa, por lo que se opone frontalmente a representar de forma unilateral a ninguna plantilla. Esta organización aspira a que las trabajadoras se agrupen y expresen a través de las secciones sindicales, para que estas sirvan como herramienta de lucha y defensa de sus intereses. Por lo tanto, con este comunicado no se ha pretendido nunca hablar por esa aparente totalidad de la plantilla que se expresa a través de las redes sociales de la empresa, sino que se hace en defensa de las compañeras que componen su Sección Sindical.

CNT rechaza el modelo de concertación y rehúye de cooptar la voz de las trabajadoras a través de comités monolíticos. Nuestra acción sindical ha ido y siempre irá orientada a emplear la Sección Sindical como fuerza de choque en la que las trabajadoras de cualquier empresa puedan organizarse de forma horizontal, tomando democráticamente todas las decisiones para impulsar la conquista de derechos en sus centros de trabajo.

Los derechos laborales no pertenecen a quienes están afiliados a un sindicato. Son derechos de todas las trabajadoras y trabajadores, independientemente de su afiliación, situación personal o posición dentro de la empresa. Por ello, la CNT defiende y vela por los derechos laborales de todas las personas trabajadoras, sin distinción. Lejos de perseguir intereses ajenos a la plantilla, nuestra labor consiste en acompañar, asesorar y respaldar a quienes ven vulnerados sus derechos, promoviendo siempre la mejora de las condiciones laborales y el respeto a la dignidad de las trabajadoras.

Consideramos de especial gravedad que los canales oficiales de la empresa hayan hecho público con semejante ligereza datos privados sobre una de nuestras compañeras, exponiendo que se encuentra en situación de baja, así como su afiliación sindical. Recordamos, además, que la significación sindical en un centro de trabajo es una decisión que compete enteramente a las trabajadoras, así como los riesgos que ha acarreado siempre a incontables compañeras hacer sindicalismo públicamente

Destacamos también que, pese al discurso y la estética de la que pueda hacer gala la empresa, esta se conforma de acuerdo con el modelo capitalista de explotación de la clase trabajadora y extracción de su fuerza de trabajo y plusvalía. Taberna Garibaldi no ejerce como cooperativa en la que las trabajadoras tomen democráticamente las decisiones e impulsen de forma horizontal y sin imposiciones el modelo de gestión en el centro de trabajo.

Esto se suma al llamativo hecho de que el comunicado aparentemente respaldado por “todas” las trabajadoras haya sido emitido desde los canales oficiales de la empresa y que, en este, se hable en términos que eluden directamente la naturaleza de la empresa y diluyen la distinción entre patronal, cargos jerárquicos, y trabajadoras.

La organización independiente de las trabajadoras, contar con sus medios de expresión y altavoces, así como sus espacios para organizarse desde los que exponer sus demandas son el único medio que puede garantizar que no existan injerencias de la patronal en la voluntad y posicionamiento de cualquier plantilla en sus centros de trabajo.

Afirmar, por otra parte, que pueda existir interés mediático tras el comunicado de este Sindicato supone poner el foco en tan solo una de las personas que ejerce la propiedad de la empresa: hecho que no se produce en ningún momento en nuestro comunicado. CNT Comarcal Sur recuerda que la propiedad de Taberna Garibaldi es ejercida por varias personas, pretender reducir la cuestión a una individualidad se aleja completamente de las palabras emitidas por este Sindicato, así como de su acción sindical: la relación sindical que esta organización pueda mantener ha sido y es siempre con la patronal de Taberna Garibaldi.

Desviar en este sentido la atención no solo aparta la mirada del conflicto existente, sino que, además, mediante la victimización de esta individualidad, se pone en juego un enorme capital político y social que ha sido volcado contra nuestra organización y compañeras. La afinidad que esta empresa pudiera tener con personalidades políticas, partidos institucionales o medios de comunicación; lejos de suponer un aliciente para la acción sindical, entraña un perjuicio constante para ejercer con libertad cualquier tipo de actividad pública dentro de los márgenes de esta empresa.

CNT Comarcal Sur, de acuerdo con sus principios, medios y fines anarcosindicalistas, se encuentra completamente al margen del juego electoralista en el que la izquierda institucional pueda verse envuelto; y no saca rédito alguno de incidir en este ámbito. La actividad de este Sindicato se despliega siempre para defender los derechos de las trabajadoras y avanzar en la lucha de clases, independientemente de cualquier partido y corriente política electoralista. La confrontación con la patronal es la premisa básica del día a día de CNT Comarcal Sur y, como puede demostrar nuestra acción reciente, frente a las absurdas afirmaciones que nos ubican “haciendo el juego a la ultraderecha”, este Sindicato ha estado en primera línea interponiendo denuncias contra el alcalde de Madrid, José Luis Martinez Almeida, por posibles delitos en el proceso de regularización extraordinaria de personas migrantes; impulsando con su Sección Sindical una escalada de conflicto en la plantilla de Equipos de Calle de Madrid que ha desembocado esta misma semana en la convocatoria de paros parciales; y lleva articulando años la lucha en la educación pública madrileña junto a organizaciones sindicales y plataformas como Menos Lectivas, entre muchas otras acciones, campañas, conflictos y trabajo de sindicalismo combativo que venimos haciendo más o menos alejado de los focos.

La acción sindical no debe entenderse como un ataque personal, sino como una herramienta legítima para garantizar condiciones de trabajo dignas. Señalar posibles incumplimientos no busca generar titulares, sino contribuir a que los derechos de las personas trabajadoras sean respetados y a demostrar que es posible organizarnos para defenderlos. Nuestros comunicados son parte de la acción sindical.

El comunicado busca crear las condiciones para que la patronal recapacite sobre la actual relación con nuestro sindicato y acceda a dialogar de forma seria y rigurosa para resolver los puntos sobre los que tenemos demandas.

La mejor repercusión posible no sería la mediática, sino aquella en la que no fuera necesario denunciar incumplimientos porque los derechos laborales se respetaran plenamente. Mientras eso no ocurra, seguiremos ejerciendo nuestra labor sindical con independencia, coherencia y compromiso con la clase trabajadora.

Defender derechos no es generar conflictos: es garantizar justicia laboral.

author: 柴思原
title: 日本簽證新規下異國餐廳危機與移民社群的未來
content:
今年五月，在東京一場集會上，在埼玉縣經營印度餐廳的Manish Kumar公開落淚，講述自己未能成功更新在留資格的經過。他在日本生活三十年、經營餐廳十八年，孩子在日本出生長大，卻面臨離境風險。雖然其個案的具體審查理由未公開，但在日本收緊經營管理簽證政策的背景下，此案迅速引發移民社群與輿論關注。

日本於2025年10月修訂經營管理簽證制度。舊制下，外籍人士只需準備500萬日圓以上資本額及基本經營計畫即可申請；新制則將最低資本額提高至3000萬日圓，並新增雇用本地全職員工及日語能力等要求。據日本媒體報導，新制實施後，經營管理簽證的月均申請件數由約1700件降至約70件，跌幅達96%。政府認為，過去部分人士透過設立空殼公司取得在留資格，提高門檻有助堵塞制度漏洞。負責「與外國人有序共生社會」政策的小野田紀美大臣亦表示，經營管理簽證被作為移民管道濫用的疑慮已在一定程度上獲得緩解。

然而，問題在於大幅提高資本要求是一種相當粗放的政策工具，難以區分空殼公司與已長期經營、正常納稅的小型企業。一家持續營運十八年、雇用員工並按時納稅的餐廳，與從未實際營運的紙上公司，在新制下適用同一套資本標準。東京商工調查於2026年春季針對299家外國人經營企業的調查顯示，超過45%的受訪企業預期新規將帶來負面影響，5%甚至考慮結束在日業務。雖然政府設有三年過渡期，但部分業者因前景不確定而提前考慮退場。

這項政策更值得關注之處，在於它與日本面臨的人口與勞動力現實形成矛盾。日本正經歷人口萎縮與高齡化，許多產業長期面臨人手不足。據估計，日本現有超過四千家以「印度咖哩」為名的餐廳，其中大部分實際由尼泊爾移民經營，不僅提供餐飲服務，也吸納大量外籍勞工，成為移民社群的重要據點。若這類企業因政策收緊而減少，不僅影響地方商業生態，也可能削弱日本對海外人才的吸引力。

更重要的是，日本近年其實正試圖建立更穩定的外籍勞工制度。2024年，政府通過法案，以新的「育成就勞制度」取代備受批評的技能實習制度，希望鼓勵外籍勞工在日本長期留任。然而，近期提高外籍企業主的定居與創業門檻，卻顯示政府對移民長期融入社會仍抱持保留態度。如何在控制移民規模、維持經濟活力與回應民意之間取得平衡，已成為日本移民政策面臨的核心挑戰。

對於簽證制度可能遭濫用的問題，加強審查並無不妥。爭議並不在於是否管理，而在於管理方式是否足夠精準。相較於一刀切地提高資本門檻，更重視企業的實際營運狀況、納稅紀錄與長期經營表現，或許更能區分真正的投機行為與已深耕社區多年的小型企業。

目前，「#推しエスニックといつまでも」（希望喜愛的異國餐廳能夠一直存在）已在社群媒體廣泛流傳，要求政府重新檢討新規的網路連署也累積近六萬個簽名。這顯示問題已不再只是移民社群的關切，而是逐漸成為日本社會討論的一項公共議題。若政府能在三年過渡期內建立更具彈性的審查標準，或許更有機會在防堵制度濫用與維繫既有社區活力之間取得平衡。

柴思原，早稻田大學政治經濟學術院副研究員，他的研究領域為政治社會學、比較政治學和公共輿論，主要關注東亞和日本。他關於日本政治和社會的評論文章曾刊登於Nikkei Asia、Japan Times、The Diplomat 、East Asia Forum和聯合早報等平台。

author: winter oak
title: Organic Libertarianism in Appalachia
content:
I think we need to seriously consider being more Appalachian.

I try to avoid using the world ‘libertarian.’

This is mainly because the primary associations of the term for Americans is different than for other people. Here the primary connotation is to a political ideology and philosophy which is a strong form of classical liberalism: individualism, negative rights, very limited government, and as many interactions as possible are to be handed over to the market to sort out.

Outside of The States the term usually has much broader resonance, being applicable to anyone who is pro-liberty; you could even be a collectivist libertarian I think, which would be seen by American libertarians as an oxymoron.

Ron and Rand Paul would typically be considered American Libertarian politicians.

However, in thinking about the political culture of Appalachia, ‘libertarian’ seems like the best term to me, but it isn’t the sort of libertarianism I usually call ‘American libertarianism’ (to avoid confusion with my European friends).

Here I would like to sort out two sorts of American libertarianism then. The first sort I think it is better to call Liberal Libertarianism (though that risks semantic redundancy) and the second sort Organic Libertarianism.

Robert Nozick (1938-2002) was a political philosopher at Harvard and his Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) is probably the best theoretical statement of Liberal Libertarianism.

In this work, Nozick was writing against the defense of the social welfare state of his Harvard colleague John Rawls’ (1921-2002) A Theory of Justice (1971). Hence, Nozick’s main focus is on the distribution of goods within a society and what role the State plays in regulating that distribution.

At the core of his theory is his conception of The Entitlement Theory of Distribution. This evaluates the justness of owning something, based on a 3-step schema:

You can own something through ‘just acquisition’ (making it or justly claiming it).

You can come to own something through ‘just transfer’ (voluntarily buying or being given it).

Finally, there is no just holding except as arrived at via one of the above two means (hence any government redistribution would need to meet some extreme criteria to justify it).

Nozick is putting forth a State of Nature sort of theory, so the starting point is the assumption of no government. Given that, what is the maximum amount of government that can be justified?

He assumes individuals within the state of nature will seek to defend their holdings (no government needed for that). He foresees people banding together to provide that for themselves collectively more effectively. This could be like a heavy-duty neighborhood watch association. Also, some groups might contract with a company to provide security services. Now, in this situation, there is no extrinsic law that either the neighbors or the security firms are operating under: they simply exist to protect property. Or, you could form them to go take other people’s property. Or if every street hires a different security firm, the employees of those could get into scuffles. Hence, it will be in the interests of everyone around the area to establish a ‘dominant association’ to provide reliable security for the protection of property.

This is the emergence of government on Nozick’s account. This represents what he terms the ‘ultra-minimal state’: a subscription service that individuals pay for to provide effective security and protection of property. Is that the extent of legitimate government? Not quite on his account. He sees that the moral justification for establishing this armed subscription service was the possession of the right to defend one’s property.

Now, there will be people who cannot afford to pay for the subscription service but who have some property (at least in their persons) that they would like defended. Can they be denied this? They can’t pay, so why get the protection? On Nozick’s view, the ‘police’ are operating according to the interests of the subscribers. He thinks that for that to be morally justified, there is a need to recognize the rights of others and to ensure they have this same level of basic protections for their property as well.

Hence, the ‘minimal’ or ‘night watchman state’ comes into being. It is proper to tax the citizenry to provide basic security services to all members. This is the only redistributive function Nozick holds is justified. Hence, no larger, more active, state can be legitimated.

I have a ton of objections to Liberal Libertarianism. Chief among them are:

I respect the rigor of Nozick’s argument and in America it will get a decent hearing because it is a modern, and extreme, version of the old Classical Liberalism which was important at our Founding. However, I’m again’ it utterly.

I think there is a more authentic, socially grounded, and workable alternative to Liberal Libertarianism which is likely to preserve genuine liberty better. To an extent, it was the dominant ‘American way’ in most places through most of our history, but it can come into especially sharp focus in the context of Appalachia.

Here we’ll look at the cultural values and religious forms characteristic of Appalachia, at least as it stood several decades ago when its cultural integrity was more fully intact.

Loyal Jones (1928-2023) was a folklorist and was considered the ‘father of Appalachian Studies.’ In his seminal essay, ‘Appalachian Values,’ he suggests that the geography of the mountains and the settlement patterns of the people who came there played a major part in the development of Appalachian culture and values. Whether they were originally from England, Scottland, Wales, Germany, France, or Africa, the settlement patterns of Appalachia suggest a people who were looking for seclusion and independence. Jones does not exclude the native Cherokee inhabitants of the southern parts of the region from that mix. He says “…we avoided mainstream life and thus became self-reliant.”

“For a people escaping from infringements of church and state,” he observes, “Appalachia was ideal for a new way of life, for a time, away from ‘powers and principalities.’” The relative isolation of the mountains provided the “freedom to do much as they pleased” because the mountains afforded land and solitude.

This isolation, combined with the fact that the first generation or two tended to eschew formal education, led to both the regional distinctiveness of the people and many of the negative stereotypes associated with them. Further, organized religion was also absent in the early decades of settlement and when the church folks eventually caught up to them it was a distinct mountain form of religion that developed (though ‘mainliners’ have insisted on sending ‘missionaries’ ever since to help civilize the people of the region).

Prior to the Northern companies coming to the region to extract its resources, primarily coal and timber, the vast majority of Appalachians were subsistence farmers. Small-holdings stretched up many of the ‘hollers’ (the relatively flat and narrow land at the base of and between mountains; also called ‘coves’ in southern Appalachia) of the region. This created natural community ties between those who lived in the same holler and natural distance from those in other holllers or the outside world more broadly.

Jones notes that the values of traditional Appalachian people are rooted in their religion and the Bible. The forms of Christianity that took root and developed in the region stemmed from The First Great Awakening. This was comprised of a faith more ‘optimistic’ than old-style Calvinism with its total depravity and denial of free-will. The newer faiths were Methodist and Free-Will Baptist in orientation. These were largely forms of religious expression created by and for the lowly members of society with a distinctly emotional aspect (what critics termed ‘enthusiasm’).

However, these movements were transformed when they moved into the mountains. Mountain people were not optimistic about human perfectibility, individually or socially. As a result, mountain religion took on both a sort of fatalism that what will be, will be, and yet a spiritual earnestness, directness, and fervor which gave pride of place to individual spiritual experience, often of a visceral sort.

Appalachians also valued independence, self-reliance, and pride above most other values. As Jones puts it, they were Americans, they were Southerners, they were rural, and they were farmers: “independence raised to the fourth power,” as he expressed it. They grew or made almost everything they needed, including their own music, of course. They didn’t need the outside world much and they wanted that world to just leave them alone for the most part.

They were also neighborly and hospitable. Part of the reason for this is that if someone came to visit you, they had probably gone through a lot of effort to get there. You needed to feed them and probably put them up for the night. Hopefully they brought their instruments with them and you could make a little music together when supper was over. Learning a new tune or playing style were possibilities. And the hosts enjoyed the company, so they expressed their appreciation with their hospitality.

The family was at the center of mountain people’s lives. Notoriously, there tended to be a lot of genealogical interconnection between the families in a holler and the other hollers nearby. They had more of an extended-family conception of family than of the nuclear family that came along later. Children would be reared in this larger, extended, kin group and it was this group that gathered on holidays or for significant events like marriages and funerals.

An additional value Jones identified was what he termed ‘personalism.’ This manifests itself in a great reluctance to offend others. The flip side of that is that if you don’t offend anyone, they got no right meddling in your business. He notes that this value extended to matters of race in a way pretty unique in the South. During the war (ie, the main one, the Civil War), Appalachians tended to be pro-Union and anti-slavery. Slavery was little practiced in the area; it did not lend itself to large-scale agriculture. Western Virginia even broke off and became its own state. People in the mountain regions of even Tennessee and northern Georgia and Alabama often fought for the Union. Confederates had a hard time moving troops or supplies through eastern Tennesse, for example. Jones presents legal segregation as a post-war “imposition” on Appalachian culture. Though that is probably a little generous.

Related to this, folks tend to be humble and modest, deflecting compliments or heightened status that would come from individual achievements. Jones states they are “levelers;” insisting they are as good as anyone else, but no better. This is reflected in the Appalachian emphasis on humor and funny story telling (also often reflected in funny folk songs). Humor is both a coping mechanism and a way of knocking those who have gotten too big for their britches down a notch or two.

Appalachian people also demonstrate a great love of place. Given the dominating influence of geography in the region, place imposes itself; one can’t help but be mindful of it. But people tend to love the mountains as well, both for their natural beauty and the way of life they have supported. It is still not unheard of to refer to one’s locale as ‘God’s Country.’

They are also patriotic. The ‘overmountain men’ (the settlers who moved over the mountains during the colonial days) largely declared their independence from the more civilized eastern settlers. They were self-consciously their own breed. When the British, during the Revolutionary War, demonstrated the ill-advised plan of moving over the mountains they were defeated at King’s Mountain by the backwoodsmen. However, like Southerners in general, Appalachians have always had high volunteer rates when the country as a whole found itself in armed conflict. Jones boasts that in Korea and Vietnam 8 or 9 percent of American soldiers were from Appalachia, but they earned 18 and 13 percent, by respective war, of Medals of Honor awarded.

However, there is something of a contradiction here as well. Given the economic turbulence introduced to the region during modernization (and the attempt to resist some of that process), people often supplemented their situation by producing and selling moonshine. This was a craft carried over and sustained from the old country. Jones assiduously avoids discussing practices tied to the hillbilly stereotype. But this was a real thing and ‘the revenue man’, often a federal official, was hated and distrusted. The Whiskey Rebellion only ended in Appalachia in the last half century. Hillbillies will volunteer to serve, but historically, they would not allow themselves to be imposed upon.

Finally, Jones notes their love for, and sense of, beauty. No doubt this stems from the rough beauty of the topography. Most Appalachian handcrafts were items designed for functional utility. However, it became very common to incorporate aesthetic attributes. This would include things like wood inlay or scrollwork on a rifle.

Or the fineness of the stitching and beauty of design of a quilt made of scrap fabric.

The picture that emerges is of a people who are not fancy or refined, but authentic, hardy, self-reliant, sociable, and who built their lives, products, and communities from the ground up in a way that expresses their unique identity.

The most important social entity, besides family, in Appalachia for most of its history was not the State or the government, or even the town, but the local church. Hence, it is here, I think, that we can get a sense of what Appalachian Organic Libertarian social institutions look like.

My guide is Bill J. Leonard and his Appalachian Mountain Christianity: The Spirituality of Otherness. He focuses on two main strands of mountain religion, the old style religion of the Primitive and Old Regular Baptists and the newer (late nineteenth and early twentieth century) Pentecostal and Holiness churches.

First and foremost, religion was a do-it-yourself sort of affair. Appalachians disliked outsiders approaching them through missionary activity. They built their own churches and denominations.

They also distrusted experts. Ministers were not chosen based on their academic qualifications. In fact, many denominations forbade seminary education. The minister was to be called by God to ministry, not by themselves or by a church hierarchy. If God called them, God, it was presumed, would equip them for the work.

This accounts for some of the distinctive preaching styles of Appalachia where the minister may become lost in thought, speaking directly to God to give him a word, perhaps entering into a sort of sing-song and back and forth with the congregation that God show him what to preach.

Further, ministers were not paid well and, again, some denominations forbade ministerial salaries altogether. You did it because you knew you had to, because ‘called,’ not as a career. That was Plato’s old move of divorcing authority from material reward or power. Paid ministers would be ‘hirelings,’ people beholden to their paychecks and those who wrote them.

Also, preaching and worship in general has a strong emotional component, a characteristic of all plebeian spirituality. This comes to the fore in Pentecostalism with speaking in tongues, dancing, and other ‘works of the spirit’.

Mountain religion also emphasized certain basics. Literalism in biblical interpretation. Acapella singing. Baptism in living (flowing) water. Keep it rooted and real, not fancy and sophisticated.

Finally, Appalachian religions placed a special emphasis on what was sometimes called the ‘third sacrament;’ foot washing.

Foot washing both humbles the individual and binds the community; mutual service.

Imagine how your place of employment would be different if everyone humbled and conjoined themselves in this way. A social revolution!

(And I didn’t even mention serpent handling.)

Hillbillies and the Faded Republic

Liberal Libertarianism was never anyone’s actual way of life. What I want to draw out is that Organic Libertarianism is actually rooted in individual and societal ways of life (Appalachia providing just one example).

The point is not to suggest that we somehow reconstitute some pristine and past mountain culture. It is that this is one more instance of a living inspiration that as Americans we have available to us to draw upon, one more branch, or even headwater, of the river which is the republic.

As this first series of essays on The Faded Republic draws near its close, that is really what all the essays have probably been about. If it is true that the past is never really dead, we ought to try to remember it sometimes, just to understand ourselves. And also, to understand some of the deep resources we have to draw upon. This opens up new but rooted options we might consider.

The world of mass media militates against that. The world of consumerism positively assaults it. For several decades, an outright ideological war has been waged against the memory of our history; making it a positive sin to remember.

It is my conviction that our republic is faded from memory, but it is my hope that it is still there.

Loyal Jones (photographs by Warren E. Brunner), Appalachian Values, The Jesse Stuart Foundation, 1994.

Bill J. Leonard, Appalachian Mountain Christianity: The Spirituality of Otherness, The University of Georgia Press, 2024.

Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia. Basic Books, 1974.

You can read all of W.D. James’ work, and listen to his musical recommendations, at his Philosopher’s Holler blog on Substack.

Excellent article, Paul! Although I’ve never been to Appalachia myself, I have people from there and done a little on the subject here and there. So much of what we now regard as quintessentially American was historically derived from or exemplified by the Appalachian culture that you’d almost assume that they must be among the most honored groups on the country. Sadly, however, they seem to be among the most despised groups on the country, despite (or because of?) that fact.

Appalachians tended to be pro-Union and anti-slavery. Slavery was little practiced in the area; it did not lend itself to large-scale agriculture … Jones presents legal segregation as a post-war “imposition” on Appalachian culture. Though that is probably a little generous.

You hit the nail on the head there: the absence of slavery in Appalachia was almost entirely a function of the fact that those mountains were unsuitable for growing cotton or other cash-crops. What agriculture occurred there was small-scale and mostly subsistence-oriented. And that is what accounted for the fact that there almost no black people there.

They are also patriotic. The ‘overmountain men’ (the settlers who moved over the mountains during the colonial days) largely declared their independence from the more civilized eastern settlers. They were self-consciously their own breed. When the British, during the Revolutionary War, demonstrated the ill-advised plan of moving over the mountains they were defeated at King’s Mountain by the backwoods.

This might surprise a lot of people, but it turns out that unlike New England and Tidewater Virginia, Appalachia was not exactly a hotbed of republican sentiment during the War of Independence. This is not because the people there held any romantic notions regarding ‘throne and altar’; rather, it was mostly a function of the fact that they associated the independence movement with the cotton barons of Tidewater Virginia, whom they saw as a far greater danger to their way of life than some distant king in London. The Appalachians must have abided by motto, ‘Better a faraway master than one close at hand’.

Incidentally, referencing your point above, this fact likely also contributed to their general disdain for secession during the Civil War, which was, once again, being most strongly pushed by those same cotton barons who now dominated the state houses of the Old South. Obviously, it also true that they had no interest in preserving slavery, owning no slaves themselves — and they surely weren’t going to die for it! But you are probably right in supposing that this all had little to do with any real sympathy for the blacks, who were largely absent from Appalachia at that time. In fact, the importation of Africans was probably one of many things they held against the Tidewater aristocracy back east. The Appalachians, in general, were far too inward-turned a people ever to believe in something like today’s ‘multiculturalism,’ which would have led them eventually to support segregation, once the issue of secession was out of the way. (Selective assimilation of the Indians, however, did sometimes occur, as you noted. But the Indians, of course, were not ‘imports’; they were already there when the first Scots-Irish arrived.)

The article is by W.D. James rather than by me but I certainly agree with you that it is a good one! Paul

author: Bindi Bennett
title: A reflection on Sorry Day and Reconciliation Week 2026
content:
It’s Sorry Day and Reconciliation week

and I’m reminded again that language matters.

White people tell me this constantly.
Use the right language.
Tone it down.
Be careful how you say it.
Be professional.
Be strategic.
Be calm.
Be nice.

And yet I keep watching white people use language as a weapon against Aboriginal Peoples every single day.

Correcting us.
Explaining us.
Gaslighting us.
Policing us.
Speaking over us.
Hiding behind policy, process, optics and “good intentions” while Aboriginal Peoples drown under colonial and cultural load.

Watching white people collect awards, promotions, praise and recognition for “anti-racism”, “equity” and “reconciliation” while Aboriginal staff are exhausted, isolated, broken and leaving institutions in pieces.

Language matters, Bindi.
But apparently Aboriginal wellbeing does not.

Apparently our pain is inconvenient if it disrupts white comfort.
Apparently racism only counts when it is obvious, historical, far away or performed by “bad people”.
Not when it is structural.
Not when it is institutional.
Not when it is hidden inside governance, complaints, exclusion, silencing, over-explaining, reputation management and defensiveness.

Why aren’t you smiling?
Why aren’t you grateful?
Why aren’t you more collaborative?
Why are you “angry”?
Why are you making this difficult?

Because I am watching people explain why the harm they are causing is not actually harm.
I am watching people intellectualise racism while Aboriginal Peoples continue to die under it.

Carefully crafted statements.
Beautiful acknowledgements.
Perfect reconciliation branding.
LinkedIn posts about justice and allyship.
Endless discussions about wording and tone while our communities are still carrying the statistics, the grief, the removals, the suicides, the burnout, the surveillance, the racism and the premature death.

And somehow the priority remains protecting white reputations rather than Aboriginal lives.

But if your language is only ever used to defend power, minimise harm, protect institutions and silence Aboriginal pain, then it is not reconciliation.

In Reconciliation Week the flags are flying. The morning teas are happening. Organisations are sharing carefully designed graphics about unity, respect and walking together. LinkedIn fills with acknowledgements, commitments and reflections on how far Australia has come.

And every year I find myself asking the same question.

What exactly are we reconciling?

Because reconciliation sounds wonderful in theory. It sounds hopeful. Generous. Forward-looking.

But reconciliation cannot simply mean Aboriginal Peoples becoming reconciled to the ongoing realities of colonisation.

It cannot mean becoming reconciled to racism and inequity.

Reconciled to the overrepresentation of our children in care, our people in prisons, our communities in poverty statistics and our families in grief.

It cannot mean becoming reconciled to systems that continue to extract from Aboriginal people while congratulating themselves for inclusion.

Yet sometimes that is exactly what reconciliation feels like.

For many Aboriginal Peoples, reconciliation has become a season rather than a transformation. A week of statements rather than a year of action. A public performance where institutions enthusiastically celebrate relationships while avoiding conversations about power.

Because power remains the uncomfortable part of reconciliation.

Everyone likes the idea of “partnership”.

Far fewer people are comfortable with sharing decision-making.

Far fewer people are comfortable when inclusion means changing systems, redistributing resources or challenging existing privilege.

Everyone likes hearing Aboriginal voices.

Until those voices become critical.

Until they challenge institutions.

Until they point out that despite decades of reconciliation efforts, Aboriginal Peoples are still carrying disproportionate cultural load, emotional labour and responsibility for fixing systems we did not create.

Then suddenly the conversation changes.

The issue is no longer the racism.

The issue becomes the way we describe the  racism .

The issue is no longer the harm.

The issue is no longer accountability.

Aboriginal Peoples learn these lessons very early.

We are often welcomed into conversations provided we remain agreeable.

We are encouraged to share our experiences provided those experiences do not make anyone too uncomfortable.

We are invited to tell the truth provided it is delivered gently enough to protect the people who benefit from not hearing it.

When we name what is happening?

We are frequently described as divisive, emotional, difficult or angry.

Aboriginal Peoples are asked to reconcile with histories and systems that have caused profound harm, while institutions often struggle to reconcile with criticism.

Real reconciliation was never supposed to be comfortable.

Truth-telling is not comfortable.

Learning that institutions you care about have caused harm is not comfortable.

Recognising your own privilege is not comfortable.

Acknowledging that good intentions can coexist with racism is not comfortable.

Yet somehow reconciliation has increasingly been reframed as a process designed to maintain comfort rather than challenge injustice.

Perhaps that is why so many Aboriginal Peoples experience a complicated relationship with Reconciliation Week.

We understand the significance of conversations, education and awareness.

But we also know awareness alone does not create change.

Aboriginal Peoples do not need more people to know we exist.

Australia already knows we exist.

The challenge has never been awareness.

The challenge has always been action.

What would reconciliation look like if we took it seriously?

It would look like Aboriginal Peoples being believed when we describe racism.

It would look like institutions addressing cultural load instead of simply celebrating cultural expertise.

It would look like accountability that extends beyond statements and symbolism.

It would look like funding decisions, governance structures and leadership pathways that reflect self-determination rather than consultation.

It would look like non-Indigenous people carrying more of the work that reconciliation currently asks Aboriginal Peoples to do.

It would look like truth-telling that is ongoing rather than annual.

Most importantly, it would involve a shift from asking Aboriginal Peoples to prove harm toward asking institutions how they intend to prevent it.

Because too often reconciliation has been positioned as something Aboriginal Peoples must participate in rather than something Australia must actively pursue.

The consequences certainly remain uneven.

As Aboriginal Peoples, we continue to show extraordinary generosity.

To participate in processes that frequently ask us to revisit painful histories while simultaneously reassuring others that they are doing their best.

That generosity should never be mistaken for an absence of frustration.

Nor should resilience be mistaken for acceptance.

The fact that Aboriginal Peoples continue showing up does not mean the work is done.

It means the work remains necessary.

So this Reconciliation Week, perhaps the question is not whether we support reconciliation.

Perhaps the question is whether we are willing to confront what genuine reconciliation actually requires.

Because reconciliation is not measured by how many acknowledgements we deliver, how many events we attend or how many social media posts we share.

It is measured by what happens when Aboriginal Peoples tell difficult truths.

It is measured by how institutions respond when confronted with racism rather than celebrated for good intentions.

It is measured by whether power shifts.

Until then, reconciliation risks becoming another beautiful word used to describe a future that never quite arrives.

And Aboriginal Peoples have waited long enough.

Professor Bindi Bennett (she/her) is a Gamilaraay woman, mother, and social worker and is a Professorial Research Fellow at Federation University living, playing and working on Jinibara lands. She is a social justice scholar, a compassionate radical and activist requesting transformational change. Her research areas are disability/neurodivergence, Remote, Rural and Regional Aboriginal wellbeing and AI in the First Nations space.

author: Bindi Bennett
title: A reflection on Sorry Day and Reconciliation Week 2026
content:
It’s Sorry Day and Reconciliation week

and I’m reminded again that language matters.

White people tell me this constantly.
Use the right language.
Tone it down.
Be careful how you say it.
Be professional.
Be strategic.
Be calm.
Be nice.

And yet I keep watching white people use language as a weapon against Aboriginal Peoples every single day.

Correcting us.
Explaining us.
Gaslighting us.
Policing us.
Speaking over us.
Hiding behind policy, process, optics and “good intentions” while Aboriginal Peoples drown under colonial and cultural load.

Watching white people collect awards, promotions, praise and recognition for “anti-racism”, “equity” and “reconciliation” while Aboriginal staff are exhausted, isolated, broken and leaving institutions in pieces.

Language matters, Bindi.
But apparently Aboriginal wellbeing does not.

Apparently our pain is inconvenient if it disrupts white comfort.
Apparently racism only counts when it is obvious, historical, far away or performed by “bad people”.
Not when it is structural.
Not when it is institutional.
Not when it is hidden inside governance, complaints, exclusion, silencing, over-explaining, reputation management and defensiveness.

Why aren’t you smiling?
Why aren’t you grateful?
Why aren’t you more collaborative?
Why are you “angry”?
Why are you making this difficult?

Because I am watching people explain why the harm they are causing is not actually harm.
I am watching people intellectualise racism while Aboriginal Peoples continue to die under it.

Carefully crafted statements.
Beautiful acknowledgements.
Perfect reconciliation branding.
LinkedIn posts about justice and allyship.
Endless discussions about wording and tone while our communities are still carrying the statistics, the grief, the removals, the suicides, the burnout, the surveillance, the racism and the premature death.

And somehow the priority remains protecting white reputations rather than Aboriginal lives.

But if your language is only ever used to defend power, minimise harm, protect institutions and silence Aboriginal pain, then it is not reconciliation.

In Reconciliation Week the flags are flying. The morning teas are happening. Organisations are sharing carefully designed graphics about unity, respect and walking together. LinkedIn fills with acknowledgements, commitments and reflections on how far Australia has come.

And every year I find myself asking the same question.

What exactly are we reconciling?

Because reconciliation sounds wonderful in theory. It sounds hopeful. Generous. Forward-looking.

But reconciliation cannot simply mean Aboriginal Peoples becoming reconciled to the ongoing realities of colonisation.

It cannot mean becoming reconciled to racism and inequity.

Reconciled to the overrepresentation of our children in care, our people in prisons, our communities in poverty statistics and our families in grief.

It cannot mean becoming reconciled to systems that continue to extract from Aboriginal people while congratulating themselves for inclusion.

Yet sometimes that is exactly what reconciliation feels like.

For many Aboriginal Peoples, reconciliation has become a season rather than a transformation. A week of statements rather than a year of action. A public performance where institutions enthusiastically celebrate relationships while avoiding conversations about power.

Because power remains the uncomfortable part of reconciliation.

Everyone likes the idea of “partnership”.

Far fewer people are comfortable with sharing decision-making.

Far fewer people are comfortable when inclusion means changing systems, redistributing resources or challenging existing privilege.

Everyone likes hearing Aboriginal voices.

Until those voices become critical.

Until they challenge institutions.

Until they point out that despite decades of reconciliation efforts, Aboriginal Peoples are still carrying disproportionate cultural load, emotional labour and responsibility for fixing systems we did not create.

Then suddenly the conversation changes.

The issue is no longer the racism.

The issue becomes the way we describe the  racism .

The issue is no longer the harm.

The issue is no longer accountability.

Aboriginal Peoples learn these lessons very early.

We are often welcomed into conversations provided we remain agreeable.

We are encouraged to share our experiences provided those experiences do not make anyone too uncomfortable.

We are invited to tell the truth provided it is delivered gently enough to protect the people who benefit from not hearing it.

When we name what is happening?

We are frequently described as divisive, emotional, difficult or angry.

Aboriginal Peoples are asked to reconcile with histories and systems that have caused profound harm, while institutions often struggle to reconcile with criticism.

Real reconciliation was never supposed to be comfortable.

Truth-telling is not comfortable.

Learning that institutions you care about have caused harm is not comfortable.

Recognising your own privilege is not comfortable.

Acknowledging that good intentions can coexist with racism is not comfortable.

Yet somehow reconciliation has increasingly been reframed as a process designed to maintain comfort rather than challenge injustice.

Perhaps that is why so many Aboriginal Peoples experience a complicated relationship with Reconciliation Week.

We understand the significance of conversations, education and awareness.

But we also know awareness alone does not create change.

Aboriginal Peoples do not need more people to know we exist.

Australia already knows we exist.

The challenge has never been awareness.

The challenge has always been action.

What would reconciliation look like if we took it seriously?

It would look like Aboriginal Peoples being believed when we describe racism.

It would look like institutions addressing cultural load instead of simply celebrating cultural expertise.

It would look like accountability that extends beyond statements and symbolism.

It would look like funding decisions, governance structures and leadership pathways that reflect self-determination rather than consultation.

It would look like non-Indigenous people carrying more of the work that reconciliation currently asks Aboriginal Peoples to do.

It would look like truth-telling that is ongoing rather than annual.

Most importantly, it would involve a shift from asking Aboriginal Peoples to prove harm toward asking institutions how they intend to prevent it.

Because too often reconciliation has been positioned as something Aboriginal Peoples must participate in rather than something Australia must actively pursue.

The consequences certainly remain uneven.

As Aboriginal Peoples, we continue to show extraordinary generosity.

To participate in processes that frequently ask us to revisit painful histories while simultaneously reassuring others that they are doing their best.

That generosity should never be mistaken for an absence of frustration.

Nor should resilience be mistaken for acceptance.

The fact that Aboriginal Peoples continue showing up does not mean the work is done.

It means the work remains necessary.

So this Reconciliation Week, perhaps the question is not whether we support reconciliation.

Perhaps the question is whether we are willing to confront what genuine reconciliation actually requires.

Because reconciliation is not measured by how many acknowledgements we deliver, how many events we attend or how many social media posts we share.

It is measured by what happens when Aboriginal Peoples tell difficult truths.

It is measured by how institutions respond when confronted with racism rather than celebrated for good intentions.

It is measured by whether power shifts.

Until then, reconciliation risks becoming another beautiful word used to describe a future that never quite arrives.

And Aboriginal Peoples have waited long enough.

She is a social justice scholar, a compassionate radical and activist requesting transformational change. Her research areas are disability/neurodivergence, Remote, Rural and Regional Aboriginal wellbeing and AI in the First Nations space.
